Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 112) to amend the Act respecting the Navigation of Canadian Waters. He said : The reason of the Bill is to allow the Department of Marine and Fisheries to provide regulations upon which all mariners on the large lakes have agreed. The rules for years have been those adopted at the convention in Belgium about ten years ago ; but on the lakes the Americans have been following their own rules and the Canadian mariners also their own rules. That has created much inconvenience, and the Canadians have come to the conclusion that they had better agree with the Americans and have the same rules of navigation on inland waters.
Will the rules be the same as those for the sea-board waters ?
No.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I intend to call the attention of the government to a matter of great importance, and in order that I may do so, I beg to move the adjournment of the House.
The matter to which I propose calling attention is the nationalization of the telephone and telegraph systems in this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A very urgent question.

A very urgent question and one which comes home to every one, and there is no time more opportune than the present. Every day's delay will increase the difficulty and involve a greater national expenditure and bring in a greater number of interests to be dealt with. The Postmaster General gave the public in a way to understand some years ago that he had such a project in view, and the Minister of Justice is on record as having pledged the government to introduce a general Act dealing with the telephone service, in which Act he was to provide for the nationalization of existing lines by the government, in so far as the trunk lines are concerned, and for the municipalization of local telephone services. So far, however, no progress has been made, and if for no other reason, I am warranted m making this motion and calling the attention of the government to their pledge. The telephone is one of the greatest conveniences of modern life. Its possibilities of usefulness and development are very great, but in order to realize these to their fullest extent, the system must be nationalized. We are confronted already with any number of difficulties in connection with the telephone service. In Ottawa the people voted for the municipalization of that service, but so far there is no provision in the law which would enable them to get a municipal system by taking over the Bell telephone system at a moderate price. Nor is there any provision to compel one telephone company to interchange its service with another, as in the case of railway companies. In Fort William and Port Arthur the people are suffering great inconvenience because of their inability to connect the first-class plant which they have established with the Bell telephone system or with the Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian Northern Railway services, because of certain monopolies'enjoved by the Bell Telephone Company. The result of this is a deadlock in these towns and in a dozen other localities in Ontario. Down in Quebec there are several private lines owned by private companies which are anxious to do business with the Bell Telephone Company on fair terms, but the latter company refuses to give them any connection. There never will be any removal of these grievances until there is a general Act regulating the telephone companies and empowering the state to take them over. The experiment of nationalizing either telegraphs or telephones is not a new one. It has proved a great success in Great Britain. Only the other day Lord Stanley, the present Postmaster General, son of a nobleman well known to the people of this country, showed that he had picked up some political ideas in America, by proposing to nationalize the telephone system. 1-Ie introduced a measure in parliament providing for the taking over of the national telephone lines in England. Here is the despatch giving the information :

Lord Stanley announced in the commons that the post office was negotiating for the purchase of the National Telephone Company. He asked for a small select committee to consider details and £3,000,000 for the work of the next live years. The post office system would cost a little under £8 per subscriber, though 90 per cent preferred the call system, at £6 10s., with penny messages. There were 110,128 miles of wire at present under London. The post office scheme would cost £2 less than the cheapest now in use. The London county council plan contemplated a plant sufficient for 40,000 subscribers, of which the post office had 15,299. The committee was given.
In London a national system is proposed, which the post office is to take over, and according to the first announcement they will give the public telephones for two pounds less per year than the public are paying to-day. But a still better instance of state ownership is to be found in Sweden, where the condition of affairs is summed up as follows :
Sweden is a sparsely inhabited country with a total population of slightly over 5,000,000. Telephones in Sweden are owned partly by private companies, but chiefly by the state-the number of instruments on the government system at the end of 1902 being 61,000, while the number on the other systems was estimated at about 30,000. This gives a telephone for every 553 of the inhabitants. As indicative of the rapid expansion of the state system it may be explained that the number of instruments in 1893 was only 16,000 and the increase in 1902 was upwards of 5,000, or nearly ten per cent. Although the capital expenditure has been about $6,700,000 the present debt on the state system is under $1,800,000, the difference of close on $5,000,000 having been paid out of surplus profits. It is evident, therefore, that in a short time Sweden will possess a valuable revenue producing asset free from all incumbrances, and which will have cost her nothing. In 1902 the gross receipts were about $1,325,000, and the working expenses under $600,000. After paying interest at 3 per cent equal to $55,000,

the new balance of $670,000 passed to the credit of the sinking fund established for the repayment of the capital. There are about 107,500 miles of telephone wires in Sweden, of which the trunk and junction wires on the government system account for nearly 40,000 miles, or about half the total length of that system. The income averages about $20 per instrument, the proportion of capital cost per instrument being about $110. Very remarkable, too, are the rates of subscription, which run from $24 in Stockholm, with a population of 305,879, down to $13.75 in the smaller towns and villages. These rates cover an unlimited local service-i.e., there are no additional charges for local calls-and they extend throughout the area of the town-the radius covered by the rates at Stockholm is about 2J miles. The minimum charge for the use of the trunk or inter-town wires is 4 cents for three minutes' conversation, and the maximum charge is 26 cents.
On', this system you could talk from Ottawa to Montreal for from four to eight cents. It now costs $1.75 from Ottawa to Toronto by this Bell system.
With such rates there need be no surprise that telephones have been popularized in Sweden to an extent unheard of elsewhere.
The advocate of municipal ownership concludes : * But it is surprising and is an illustrative commentary on some of the arguments in use by opponents of public ownership and management that the Swedish government officials can in the circumstances produce such extraordinarily successful financial results.'
Mr. Speaker, my contention is that now is the time to nationalize the telephone and telegraphs of this country. At the present moment the telephone service is very poor, very unsatisfactory, no provision made for interchange of service, no regulation of tolls. The investment of the Bell and other companies is constantly increasing, making it all the harder to take these services over. And yet, this is one of the great conveniences of to-day, and the nationalization of the system was made a success in Sweden, in England and in other countries of Europe. The use of the telephone is being hindered all over Canada, by our present laws on this subject. I know farmers all over this country who would build independent lines if they thought they could get connection with the trunk line, and if they thought they could get connection with the railway station. But, so far, the law is such that the Bell Company is entrenched in a position that makes it a monopolist of this important service. Not only do I wish to remove this monopoly, but I wish to see something substituted for it on the lines of state ownership. It would cost but a small amount of money, and that it can be made profitable is a certainty. A national service can be given for one-half what is charged to-day, and the revenues will provide a sinking fund that, in twenty years will extinguish the debt, as it is being done in Sweden. That being the ease, why should we delay ? I suppose it will be said that this is in the direction Mr. MACLEAN.	i
of socialism. But that kind of socialism, I take it, is good for the country. It has proven successful everywhere it has been tried. Even in Canada, where the trial has been made, the results have been most satisfactory. It is more than successful in Port Arthur and Fort William. The city of Toronto is ready-and I appeal to the representatives of that city to say if I am not right- to municipalize the Bell system, to buy out that system at a fair value, if, in taking it over, it can get the use of the trunk lines. The position is somewhat the same in Ottawa to-day. There is an unfortunate condition of affairs here. Two companies are applying for the franchise. Nobody believes in rival telephone service in a town, except when no other remedy is possible. It is well to have one system ; it is better to have that system municipalized ; but it is best of all to have it made public property in the interest of municipalities and the government together. Here is a progressive measure, the carrying out of which will cost very little money and one on which I intend, a little later on, to take the opinion of the House. And so I give the government notice that at the first opportunity offered me when the House goes into Supply, I propose to present a motion to the House in favour of the nationalization of both telegraphs and telephones.
As for telegraphs, the government of every country in Europe almost, has made an enormous success of nationalizing this system, mainly in connection with the post office. They have cut the rates in two, doubled the number of words allowed for a fixed fee, extended the mileage, opened telegraph offices in every post office and in every little hamlet where there are private companies, refused to operate them and, with all, have made the system financially successful.
Public ownership will give every farmer in Canada who wants it a telephone in his house at $8 or $10 a year, and he cannot get it to-day at less than from $40 to $100. I know cases where farmers have been asked from $100 to $150 a year for connection with the Bell telephone service. If we can give every farmer in Canada who desires it a telephone in his house for $8 a year, and business men in towns and cities a telephone at $20 a year, as they have in other countries, let^us try to do it. Consider what a convenience a telephone is. It is away ahead of railway travel, l'ou can do more business by telephone than by personal interview. I can sit in my office in Toronto and, if I want to do business in Montreal, I can call up ten men within an hour. If I wished to interview those men personally it would take me a night's journey to Montreal and a night's journey back by rail, and it would take me all day in a cab to go round, and then I could not make the connection. Yet, if the telephone was under the control of the state,

I could, by an expenditure of two or three dollars, call up these people and do my business in a much more satisfactory way. True, you can do it to-day, but you do it at great expense, and, while this convenience is available to the people in the city, it is not available to the people scattered all over the country. A progressive government would have taken this up long ago. A Postmaster General who was following what the heads of postal system^ in other countries are doing could have taken it up long ago. A Minister of Justice who had promised to give relief with regard to the telephone situation, if he had studied the situation and desired to keep his pledge, would have brought in a Bill long ago curing these grievances, either on the line of a general Act regulating the telephone system, or by an Act making the telegraphs and telephones the property of the state. In view of the fact that all these grievances d.o exist to-day, that the towns of Port Arthur and Fort William are crying for relief, that the city of Toronto is crying for relief, that the farmers all over the country are desirous of using the telephone and demanding that they shall be free to use it on reasonable terms, it is time that something should be done. Why the same conditions exist in Quebec that we find in Ontario. A gentleman from the province of Quebec told me the other day that they already have miles and miles of independent lines in Quebec, and would build them all over if they could get access to the railway station, or if they could get a connection with the Bell system,
They can get it.
How ?
Private lines have access to the railway stations along the line *of the Intercolonial, and that is the only railway we have in our district.
But we have the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway in our district.
But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) was talking about the province of Quebec.

I say that a gentleman from the province of Quebec came to me the other night-he is a man who is interested in telephones-and told me that they would extend the telephone lines greatly all over Quebec if they could get the use of the trunk lines for a reasonable toll. The Intercolonial is not the only railway in the province of Quebec. The Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific Railway are there also. Of course you can get into communication with the Bell people. But what I mean by a connection with the Bell system is not that somebody will take your message and carry it across tbe
way and hand it over to the person in charge of the Bell office, but that the Bell shall be obliged to give direct telephonic connection and charge a fee, of course ; but let that fee be under government regulation. But they do not propose' to do that. They propose to hold the people of Canada under monopoly as long as they can do it. And there is no way to break that monopoly and extend the use of the telephone except by nationalizing the trunk lines and making provision for the municipalities to take over the local services. Having said so much, I conclude by repeating the notice that I have given to the government, that, at the first opportunity I have on the motion for the House to go into Committee of Supply, I shall introduce a motion in favour of public ownership of telegraphs and telephones.

My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) has given us notice that on some future day he will refer to this matter again. I will be very thankful indeed if he will be kind enough to give us the reference to that portion of any speech which I ever made in which I promised to bring in a Bill to provide for the nationalization of telephone lines.
I did not say he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh !

I said the Minister of Justice had promised a general Act regulating telephones and I would take it for granted that one of its provisions would provide for regulations of that kind. The hon. gentleman surely cannot withdraw the statement he made in 1902 that he would bring in a general Act for the regulation of telephones.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I brought in a general Act in 1902, which together with the Bill introduced by my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) was referred to a special committee. The result was that both Bills were held over in order that they might be referred to the union of municipalities, represented by their mayors. These gentlemen met in my office and I am sorry that I did not receive notice of my hon. friend's intention to make this speech to-day so that I might have brought here the stenographic report of the proceedings at that conference. The country might be enlightened by the position taken by the municipalities. The report shows that you cannot find two mayors of two municipalities to agree on what we should do. It cannot be said that there is any general opinion among them in favour of the nationalization of telephones. I never heard an opinion expressed, except by my hon. friend, in favour of the nationalization of telegraph and telephone lines. I never heard such an opinion expressed in this House ;

why does not my hon. friend bring in such a measure ?

I cannot introduce a measure involving an expenditure of money. The hon. gentleman is paid to study the progress of events throughout the world and he must see what they are doing in England, in Sweden, in Australia, and in fact in all countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Possibly my hon. friend will tell us the deficit in connection with the operation of the national telephone system in England in the last two or three years ?
There has not been any.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a positive statement made with knowledge by my hon. friend is it ?
Yes.

It seems to me that the situation to-day requires some interference either by state ownership or otherwise to secure to the public what they have undoubtedly a right to expect, that is equal treatment by corporations and the strict fulfilment of the duties which these corporations assume when they are given a certain right of eminent domain. They are given these rights in the interests of the public and these rights should be used for the benefit of the whole public, not for a portion of it, not in favour of one individual as against another or in favour of one corporation as against another. What we have seen during the last few months seems to give a special emphasis to this necessity at the present time. Look at the fight Port Arthur is putting up for the right to put its telephones into the Canadian Pacific Railway station there, a right which is improperly, and I think illegally, denied by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Following that is the application made to the Railway Commission and the decision which they have given upon that question, which, it seems to me, justifies the immediate interference by parliament to protect the people and to secure to them the rights to which they are entitled.
A very eminent authority, Black's Constitutional Law, in dealing with this question says :
The right to exercise this power may be delegated by the legislature to private corporations

	'
That is the right of eminent domain.
-which, although their business is pursued for purposes of gain, yet stand in such a relation to the public that they may be considered as promoting the public convenience, or discharging a public office or duty, or carrying on works which are of general public utility.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then he goes on to say :
It is entirely proper, and in accordance with the principles of the constitution, that municipal corporations should be authorized to exercise the power of eminent domain for the benefit of their own restricted ' public.' . . . . The power of eminent domain can be exercised only in pursuance of legislative authority, and on the occasions and in the modes designated by the legislature, statutes authorizing the exercise of this power will be strictly construed-
A corporation gets its authority under a statute, and that gives it certain rights which it is to exercise in the interests of the general public and not in the interest of one as against the other. This constitutional authority lays down the law that these Acts must be strictly construed according to the authority that is granted to them.
-and those charged with the execution of the power will be held to a strict compliance with all the conditions and requirements of the statute. '
The right is given to a railway corporation under a statute to take over private property for the purpose of discharging its functions in the interests of the people. That right is, given to it under the authority of its franchise. Its franchise provides that it shall use these rights for the whole public and that every member of the public will have an equal interest in it, and that it will not be used to the detriment of one against another or of any company as against another. When they do that I respectfully submit they are going beyond the powers which they possess under the law.
It is also for the state, by its legislative body, to determine when the exigency arises which will justify calling this power into exercise. And it may likewise determine the specific objects to which it shall be directed.
Then further on he says :
Thus, if the charter of a corporation gives it the right to appropriate private property for certain enumerated purposes, it will possess no authority to take land for any other purposes.
Further he says :
The purpose for which the power of eminent domain is to be exercised must be public and not merely for the benefit of a private person.
Then he goes on further to say :
It must be also for the whole people, notwithstanding one or more individuals may be peculiarly and directly benefited. The purpose must be also within the sphere of the government exercising the power.
Now I simply refer to this to show that when the legislature exercises the power to give over the right of eminent domain to these corporations it gives that power to the corporation so that it may be used not for its private purposes but in the interest of the whole public and that the public must be treated alike with regard to it and that the company cannot exercise it in the interests

of one individual or one corporation to tlie detriment or the disadvantage of others. Now is that not exactly the case to-day? We have telephone lines springing up all over the country. I shall give an example in my own section. A private telephone line is being built there to-day which will be about 30 miles in length. It passes through several important villages and most of the business men in these villages do their business at the Canadian Pacific Railway station. That Canadian Pacific Railway station has a Bell telephone in it and the company will not allow the private company to place a telephone in the station. Now that railway corporation received a right and that right was to be exercised in the interests of the whole public. What right has that corporation to say that one individual who requires to do his business with the railway company shall not receive the same advantage as another individual ? I take the business men living along this line. I take the villages of Heathcote, Duncan, Kimberly and Wode-house, all of them within a radius of 20 miles through which this telephone line will pass.
Business men wish to receive information from that station, hut they will not he allowed to put a telephone into the station so that they may receive that information, because, forsooth, the Bell Telephone Company has acquired a monopoly of the right to do business through that station. The station was put there in compliance with the 'authority that was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway to do something in the interest of the public-the whole public -equitably as between and another. Then I say why has this corporation allowed a monopoly to one company and shut out all others ? But that is one Instance. There is another private telephone line extending a distance of twelve miles and passing through two very important villages. It connects large sawmills with the village of Markdale. They desire to connect this business with the railway station at Mark-dale but they will not be allowed to connect with the station because the Bell Telephone Company has a monopoly of the business there. Then, from Shelburne there are two or three lines extending for several miles east and west of the railway line. The merchants in the villages with which the telephone line connects wish to do business at the station. They desire to ascertain whether any goods have arrived for them, whether there is any freight consigned to them before they send out teams to Shelburne, to get it, but they are not allowed to get this information unless first they send a message to a private individual who will go into the station and make inquiries. I hold that should not be the case, but that these merchants should have the same right to secure information from the railway station as every user of the Bell Tele-90	'
phone Company's lines. That station has been put there for the benefit of the public and in connection with a public utility granted by the authority of this legislature, this company cannot set up one member of the community as against another. I have heard the threat made by a station agent that he would put an individual out of the grounds and that if he put his foot upon the station property he would become a trespasser which shows the very high handed way in which some people will act when they think they have a little authority. They have no more right to make such a threat to an individual upon the station ground than they would if that individual were on the highway. But they seem to think that they have the right to treat the public in a tyrannical way to the detriment of one and for the benefit of another and to prevent the people receiving the benefit from a public utility which they are entitled to receive and which it was intended they should receive when it was granted to this railway corporation. The result of the decision of the Railway Commission lately is that the people of Port Arthur cannot get their telephone into the station unless they pay a consideration for it as damages to the Bell Telephone Company. Does it not seem absurd that that should be so ? Does it not seem that we are a long-suffering people or we would demand and insist on parliament taking steps to bring these public corporations to their senses so that they would treat the public all alike. There is an urgent demand that some control shall be exercised over these corporations so that they may use their franchises for the benefit of the whole public and not for the benefit of a portion of it. It is these very questions which are so rapidly educating public sentiment up to the pitch that the people will demand that these utilities shall be taken over by the state so that the public will secure the benefits which they expected to-secure and to which they are entitled to assume they have a right to secure, but which they cannot obtain until means are found for controlling these corporations. This incident forces on the question of state ownership and state ownership mill be the ultimate destiny in this matter so that we may secure to the public the rights to which they are entitled. Events are rapidly shaping themselves in that direction. A large percentage of the whole of these telephone lines are private lines hut they are lines that are given over to the benefit of the public and they are intended to be used for the benefit of the public. These private corporations do not object to telephone lines being put into their offices so as to exchange messages. The telephone companies ought to be compelled to exchange messages just the same as railway companies are compelled to exchange

traffic. Wlien we give a railway company authority to become a common carrier it carries with it the obligation to treat the public fairly and to exchange traffic from one line to another. In like manner when we give a company power to build a telephone line it ought to carry with it the same authority, the same right and the same obligations and if it does that it will be better in the interest of the country and beter in the interest of the corporation as well.

That is all in section 2 that we can deal with just at present, hut I want to say one or two words on another matter. There has been a good deal of complaint from Canadian engineers and surveyors that they are being overlooked in the surveys made by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that citizens of the United States, who possess no better qualifications, are being employed in this

work. The complaint is perhaps somewhat aggravated by the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, or the Grand Trunk Company, I do not know which, has been making surveys over that portion of 1he line which extends eastward from Winnipeg, a portion oif the line upon which one would have supposed that the surveys would have been made by the government. These complaints have been brought to the attention, I think, of most members of the House, and I understand that they have also been placed before the government in a very formal way. If what has been said on the subject is correct, it seems to me that it should demand some intervention from the government, or at least some explanation to the House as to why it is that not only on that portion of the line which is to be constructed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, but also on a portion of the line which is to be constructed by the government, Canadian citizens have been placed very much in the background, and citizens of the United states are doing the work which our own people are fully qualified to perform. I do not know, of course, to what extent the complaints are justified by the facts ; but it is a matter on which we should have some declaration from the government. If we have in Canada men who are as fully qualified to perform this work, and I 'believe we have, as citizens of the United States, there seems to be no good reason why their claims should be overlooked, or why they should be compelled to seek their livelihood In other occupations, while the work is being performed by men brought from across the line by one or other of these companies ; especially in view of the fact that we are confronted in the United States with an alien labour law, which prevents our people from going there under contract to perform labour, and also in view of the fact that we have in this country a somewhat similar enactment which is designed to give a corresponding protection to the people of this country. I would ask. therefore, whether or not complaints of this character have been brought to the attention of the government, whether they have made any investigation, whether the complaints are well founded, and, if so, what explanation the government have to offer, and what remedy they propose ?
Sir WILFRID LAURIEiR. The matter to which my hon. friend has just made allusion was brought to the attention of the House some time ago. We received a circular from some association of engineers, which was distributed largely, I think, amongst the members of the House. Upon the receipt of that circular, we applied to Mr. Hays, manager of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and he gave a very emphatic denial to the assertions made. Mr. Hays wrote to me that of the parties of engineers employed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company at the present time over 961
97 per cent were Canadian and British subjects, and less than 3 per cent were American. I handed over this correspondence to my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Labour, who has been in further correspondence with Mr. Hays on this subject, and who, I think, will be able to give more information upon it than I can.

Since my hon. friend brought up the matter I have sent to the department for the file of correspondence up to date, and perhaps my hon. friend will allow the matter to remain in abeyance for a few minutes until the correspondence arrives, when I will read it to the committee, and it will throw some light on the attitude of the government and the position of the facts in regard to this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We can take up the subject later on, as soon as we have the correspondence.
The Minister of Labour will perhaps remember that I moved for a copy of the correspondence.
The order was only passed on Thursday or Wednesday.

I am not saying that there has been any undue delay. I only say that, under the circumstances, the correspondence might perhaps be brought as soon as possible.
Section 2 of the Bill allowed to stand.
On section 3 of the Bill,
3. The directors of the Grand Trunk Company may from time to time, and as often as they deem necessary, enter into an agreement or agreements with the directors of the Pacific Company respecting the manner and the terms upon which the Grand Trunk Company shall or may aid or assist the Pacific Company in carrying the scheduled agreements into effect, and also respecting the consideration to he given by the Pacific Company to the Grand Trunk Company under the terms of any such agreement or agreements, and may guarantee the bonds, debentures or other securities of, the Pacific Company, and perform such other services for the Pacific Company as are agreed upon, and the Grand Trunk Company may receive and take as the consideration, in whole or in part, to be given to it under the terms of any such agreement, shares of the capital stock of the Pacific Company for such amount and upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon.

I beg leave to move in amendment that the following words be added to this section :
Every such agreement shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, and a certified copy of every such agreement shall forthwith be deposited with the Secretary of State for Canada.
This is a very important concession that the government are giving to the company, and I think it is one on which we should have further explanation from the govern-

ment. We were told by the Finance Minister last session, when the original contract was under consideration, that a portion of the $45,000,000 of stock would he retained toy the government as a guarantee to the Canadian people for the fulfilment of the contract. Now we are asked to change that entirely, so that for any assistance which the old Grand Trunk Company shall give to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company it shall have the right to receive Grand Trunk Pacific stock. I will read :
And the Grand Trunk Company may receive and take as the consideration, in whole or in part, to he given to it under the terms of any such agreement, shares of the capital stock of the Pacific Company for such amount and upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon.
This is giving very great powers to these two companies, which are but one company after all, so far as the Canadian people are concerned. We have been unable to get the government to connect the old Grand Trunk Company with the new company for the purpose of fulfilling this contract. What we are asking for by this amendment is that when these two companies shall enter into such agreements as they have power to enter into under clause 3 of the original Bill, such agreements shall be submitted to and receive the approval of the Governor in Council. It seems to me that that is quite a reasonable request. The opposition contended last session that clause 3 was pretty liberal to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we are anxious now that no agreement shall be entered Into toy the two companies-which are but one after all-without the Governor In Council having the right to say whether such agreement is in the interests of the people. Bear in mind, Sir, that the Grand Trunk .Railway have their head office in London, England. It would be quite possible for the Grand Trunk Pacific to send a representative over, and the two companies might enter into an agreement without the consent and knowledge of the government. I think the clause we propose is one which the government should accept. I cannot conceive how the right hon. gentleman or his cabinet should be willing that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company should have the power to enter Into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company without first submitting that agreement for the approval of the Governor in Council. This matter was fully discussed last session and has also been discussed this session, and I do not wish to detain the committee further. I cannot refrain, however, from expressing my opinion that the Minister of Railways should be in his place to explain these matters to the Canadian people. When the right the hon. leader of the House introduced this supplemental agreement, he did so in a very polished manner. He endeavoured to create the impression that there was no very great difference between the old and the new agreement ;

but when we come to investigate we_ find enormous responsibilities and liabilities placed upon the Canadian people, through the failure of the government to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to fulfil the agreement which we passed last session. I do not wish to use strong language, or I would say it is a disgrace to the government to have the Minister of Railways come in and go out of this House from time to time without taking the slightest interest in this important agreement, which ought to be specially in his department, and which is imposing such ^enormous liabilities on the shoulders of the people. We were told that this was a business government, and as evidence we were pointed to the selection of an expert farmer to fill the post of Minister of Agriculture, and consequently we have the right to presume that in selecting a Minister of Railways the government did so because of his knowledge of railway matters. We have the opinion of the hon. gentleman who lately occupied the position of Minister of Railways reflecting on the government for having entered into this agreement, and now we have his successor, not attacking the agreement it is true, hut not taking the slightest interest in it. He evidently does not consider it worth his while to put upon record his opinion as to whether the changes proposed are in the interests of the people or not. In my opinion, when the government come to explain their policy to the people, they will find it difficult to account for this extraordinary conduct of their Minister of Railways. The amendment I have submitted Is one on which we are entitled to have the opinion of that hon. gentleman, yet he is as silent as if he had no existence. I am confident, however, the hon. minister's silence will not receive the approval of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On closer observation my hon. friend will see that clause 3, which we are now considering, has not been made necessary by anything contained in the amendments. Its object is purely and simply to give to the Grand Trunk Railway the authority to do those things which the original contract requires it to do. For instance, it is obligatory on the Grand Trunk Pacific to obtain the endorsation of the Grand Trunk Railway with respect to the first and second issue of bonds, hut the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway has, under its charter and existing legislation, no authority to give this endorsation. In addition, the Grand Trunk Railway has to take over a certain portion of the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and this provides for giving authority to the Grand Trunk Railway to do that. There are other obligations which the Grand Trunk Railway must assume. For instance, the Grand Trunk Pacific had to deposit $5,000,000 before its organization was completed, before its stock was issued, or anything done. It was therefore absolutely necessary that it should obtain the

money necessary to comply with the conditions of the contract. That money was obtained with the aid of the Grand Trunk Railway and could not have been obtained otherwise. In addition, it will be necessary for the company, during the progress of the work, to finance the undertaking. Under the terms of the original contract, there is no obligation on the part of the government to come to the assistance of the company until the whole work is completed. The government may come to its assistance, but is not obliged to do so. But during the construction of the work and pending its completion, it will be necessary to finance the undertaking, and the Grand Trunk Pacific will require aid, and this clause is intended to give the Grand Trunk Railway authority to come to its assistance. With respect to the amendment, there is one part which I think ought to be accepted, namely, the part which provides that the agreements should be- deposited with the Secretary of State, so that the country may know the character of these agreements and their contents ; but that they should be submitted to the Governor in Council for approval, is not necessary. No benefit or advantage could be derived from that. My hon. friend will remember that in the Joint Stock Company's Act it is provided that paid up stock may be issued in payment of real estate, which maybe held for the purposes of a company, and in that event, if stock is issued for that purpose, provision is made that the agreement under which the stock is taken must be deposited with the Secretary of State. There is no provision for confirmation of the terms of the agreement ; but for the convenience of the general public, the agreement must be submitted to the Secretary of State, and I am disposed to accept the amendment to that extent.
The hon. minister tells us that the government are prepared to accept the unimportant part of my amendment, but the important part, the part in which we are most interested they refuse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the last part is very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are mere domestic arrangements between the two companies in which we are not interested. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) himself has pointed out that they may be of a mere temporary character and may not last a month.
But they are about handing over the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will deal with that under another amendment. It is absolutely necessary that this company should be in a position to deal with its stock. If. it is not, I do not see how it is ever to finance its enterprise. Where is the money to come from ? We have $5,000,000 of their money in our possession, and they have to provide from that for stock. They have no available assets and will not have. They v ill have to provide $20,000,000 of rolling stock. Where is that to come from ? They will have to provide for any deficiency with respect to the second issue of bonds, for that issue cannot possibly realize par. They will have to provide for terminals, for telegraph lines, for telephone lines for ships-for all manner of things. They cannot do this otherwise than from stock. They must realize the cash to enable them to do the things which power is given them to do by their Act of Incorporation.

I understand the Minister of Justice to say that clause 3 of this Bill is not inserted in consequence of any change in the agreement ? That being so, I would like to know why any thing more was required than clause 7 of the Act of last year ? That clause enabled the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada to acquire, hold, guarantee, pledge and dispose of stocks, bonds and so on of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Why is anything more necessary in this Bill ? I think we need some further explanation from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps it would be more in line if I were to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) to point out in what respect this goes further than the clause of last year. It seems to me a modification of the power conferred on the 1 company by last year's Bill.

That is pretty much the point I am making. We ought not to pass and re-pass clauses year after year. If there is nothing more intended than there v, as last year, what was the need of passing it over again ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only difference between this clause and the clause of last year is in the concluding lines, in the words, ' The Grand Trunk Company may receive and take as a consideration, in whole or in
part	shares of the capital stock
of the Pacific Company.' In effect, they had that under the old statute. They want it in the present form, and I see no objection.

I thought that was the reason. I can imagine just how the new clause came to be inserted. We discussed clause 7 last yeftr at considerable length. Several gentlemen on this side pointed out that, under the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific coupled with the section of the Transcontinental Bill, it was quite possible for the Grand Trunk Pacific to hand over to the Grand Trunk Company, as paid up stock, any amount of capital stock of that company without receiving a dollar for it, giving it for some privileges or what the two parties chose to call privileges. But the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) pooh-poohed that idea. He was very emphatic ; said it was absolute nonsense-I think he went as far as that-to suppose that the Grand Trunk were not going to pay the value of the stock, and that they would have to pay the market value. How the Grand Trunk was to pay the market value of a stock which had not been on the market, stock that it was to acquire before it got on the market, we did not quite understand. But there was this difficulty, that the right hon. gentleman's argument was a solemn declaration from the Prime Minister that the Grand Trunk would have to pay for the stock. I have no doubt the Grand Trunk were rather concerned about taking stock after that declaration, and so they have come here now and have asked for this new clause with this little sentence at the tail end of it, providing that they may take stock in consideration of the guarantees that they are going to enter into ; the very thing we said last year that they intended to do. The Grand Trunk feared, and very properly feared, that the words used by the Prime Minister would put them in a very awkward position if they attempted to hold the stock, that they would probably run the risk of being put by the parliament of Canada in precisely the same position as any other subscriber of stock, that is, subject to calls of one hundred cents on the dollar. Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, in the correspondence that has been laid upon the table, pointed out the necessity for an understanding about the terms upon which the Grand Trunk were going to acquire that Mr. FITZPATRICK.
stock. No agreement has been entered into on that score-we have asked for it over and over again-but it was pointed out in the correspondence as an essential thing to be settled. And it is to be settled by this innocent-looking clause which, the Minister of Justice tells us, refers to mere domestic arrangements between the companies, merely a ' domestic arrangement ' involving $45,000,000 of capital. This the minister thinks is a ' domestic ' arrangement that the country is not concerned in. Why should the .government take any interest or have any care with regard to the terms upon which $45,000,000 shall rank as paid up capital against this company ? Well, Sir, I think the hon. gentleman from Peel (Mr. Blain) was quite right in moving his amendment. We do not hope-we cannot hope with such a majority against us-to prevent this clause passing. But we say that the government of Canada should have opportunity to know exactly how many millions the Grand Trunk are going to get from the Grand Trunk Pacific for these arrangements and guarantees, and they should not be allowed to receive these millions without the approval of the government of Canada.
The people of Canada are interested in it and the government ought to be interested in it, and should be compelled, even against their wishes, to look into this matter and see that no unreasonable or unjust bargain is made between these two companies that will and must injure the people, out of whose pockets sooner or later the dividends on this stock will come through the rates they will have to pay on the railway. What object have they in creating $45,000,000 of stock unless they are going to receive dividends ? The hon. gentleman says they will have to sell the shares in order to do certain things. How are they to sell unless they are going to pay dividends, and who is to draw the line as to dividends ? The charter of the company says it will be paid-up stock. What does paid-up stock amount to ? One hundred cents on the dollar. The Grand Trunk will have obtained that stock in consideration of its having guaranteed $15,000,000 worth of bonds, and having obtained the stock without paying a dollar, it will sell it, and where will the money go ? Into the coffers of the Grand Trunk Pacific ? No, into the treasury of the Grand Trunk. It will be the property of the old Grand Trunk, stock belonging to it, that will be sold, and the proceeds of the sale will not go into the treasury of the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is what the hon. gentlemen are enabling the two companies to carry out as a domestic arrangement. The Grand Trunk will be able to take the proceeds of the sale of that stock even to pay dividends on Grand Trunk Railway stock. It will be their own money. There cannot be any question about this, and hon. gentlemen know it. The Grand Trunk Railway are not going to sell stock belonging to the Grand Trunk

Pacific Company, but to the Grand Trunk Railway, and the Grand Trunk Railway will take the proceeds. Does the minister suppose that after becoming the owners of that [DOT] stock, and selling it, selling their own property and receiving the proceeds the Grand Trunk Railway is going to use the money in building branch lines or buying ships for the Grand Trunk Pacific ? No, they will use that money for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Railway proper ; it will be its own money and it is a mere pretense to say that this stock will be sold to enable any of these works to be carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Despite the intimate knowledge that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) possesses of every detail of this agreement and of every line of the contract and of the Bill for the incorporation of the Grand Trunk Pacific he deliberately tells the committtee that this stock will be sold or handed over to the Grand Trunk Company and that not one single dollar will ever be paid for it. He says that in the light of the fact that he knows, must know and does know that $5,000,000 has been put up by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company as security for the carrying out of the conditions of the contract. Where does that money come from ? Where did the Grand Trunk Pacific get that money ? How can they possibly expect to return it out of their assets ? Must that money not necessarily come out of the company? Now as to the construction of the road assuming the position which we take to be correct- as we hold it is and has not been very firmly denied by hon. gentlemen opposite- that they must provide equipment to the extent of $20,000,000. Where do the $20,000,000 come from ? How are they to be provided ? Assuming that the bond issue is not more than sufficient to enable the road to be constructed, that is the bond issue to the extent of $50,000 a mile on the mountain section and $20,000 a mile on the prairie section and as hon. gentlemen opposite have argued that the first issue guaranteed by the government will not realize more than 90 cents on the dollar how much will the second issue guaranteed by the Grand Trunk realize ? Can it be expected that it will realize more than 80? Where is the amount required to make it up to 100 to come from ? It can come out of nothing but the company's capital. Where are they to obtain money to provide, for instance, for terminal facilities, and to provide the thousands of miles of branch lines which they have to construct? Where is that money to come from except from the $45,000,000 of capital ? I say. so far as this contract is concerned, read in the light of the .Act of incorporation and of existing legislation which requires that the capital stock issue shall be limited to $45,000,000, that to carry out the purposes
for which this company is brought into existence $45,000,000, even if every dollar's worth of stock is sold at 100 cents, will not be sufficient to do it. The hon. gentleman with the great authority he possesses in this House makes statements which it seems to me are at variance with the facts. If he reads section 11 he will find that they have no right to give away anything ; they have no right to give away their stock for nothing. They have no right to give it away, they must get a dollar or a dollar's worth in exchange. The hon. gentleman's statement is entirely at variance with section 11 of the Act of incorporation. What does section 11 say ? And unless they have the authority under section 11 to dispose of this stock the stock must be subscribed for and paid in full. That is the general law under our Railway Act, so that unless they get authority under section 11 they cannot dispose of it at all. Section 11 provides :
The directors of the company elected by the shareholders may make and issue as paid up stock, shares in the Company, whether subscribed for or not, and may allot and hand over in payment for plant, rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials of any kind, or as consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired, and also for the bona fide claims of contractors and engineers, such an amount of such common stock as shall be a fair and bona fide value for the property purchased, or for the rights, powers and privileges acquired, or services rendered, as aforesaid, other than promotion services, due regard being had to the then market value of the stock. ******
This clause, down to ' engineers and contractors ' with the exception of the words ' rights, powers and privileges acquired ' is the law as we have it up to last year. They have not the power under this clause to hand over their stock, without consideration so that while they have under this clause authority to hand over their stock for other consideration than money considerations I say that the result of the Act of incorporation and of the obligations under the contract will be that in order to carry out their contract and the obligations that they assume under this. Act of incorporation, it will be necessary if they do not get 100 cents on the dollar in cash to get what is contemplated by section 11, something equal in value to 100 cents on the dollar.
I followed the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice as closely as possible and it seems to me that the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company either did not know what he was talking about when addressing his shareholders or the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice do not in any way accord with the remarks of the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Bet us see what he says in regard to these $25,000,000 of stock. After speaking of some

slight obligations which he says the Grand Trunk Railway Company incurred, he continues :
I must not forget to mention that in return for the support which we ask you to accord to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the Grand Trunk Company will retain a controlling interest in that company, and will become the possessors of the whole of the common stock, amounting to $25,000,000 or £5,000,000.
He again goes on to say :
What may be the prospective value of that security, or when it may acquire a substantial value, I cannot precisely predict, hut you must bear in mind the certain and rapid development, of the Northwest on the one hand, and the actual and very profitable results on the other hand.
The hon. the Minister of Justice says that this $25,000,000 of stock is to be held by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for the purpose of raising the money to expend on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway when it is clearly shown by Sir Rivers-Wilson that this $25,000,000 of stock is to be handed over absolutely to the Grand Trunk Railway Company as its return for some slight obligations which it incurs. The hon. the Minister of Justice says that it cannot be handed over except for cash, that there is to be an equivalent in cash given for this stock. The legislation which we are dealing with now-and I might just refer the hon. the Minister of Justice to clause 3 of the present Bill-gives to the Grand Trunk Railway Company the very power it wants to take over this $25,000,000 of stock simply for guaranteeing some bonds and giving some other slight concessions to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Section 3 is as follows
The directors of the Grand Trunk Company may from time to time, and as often as they deem necessary, enter into an agreement or agreements with the directors of the Pacific Company respecting the manner and the terms upon which the Grand Trunk Company shall or may aid or assist the Pacific Company in carrying the scheduled agreements into effect, and also respecting the consideration to be given by the Pacific Company to the Grand Trunk Company under the terms of any such agreement or agreements, and may guarantee the bonds, debentures or other securities of, the Pacific Company, and perform such other services for the Pacific Company as are agreed upon, and the Grand Trunk Company may receive and take as the consideration, in whole or in part, to be given to it under the terms of any such agreement, shares of the capital stock of the Pacific Company for such amount and upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon.
Under that clause of the Bill it is perfectly competent for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to enter into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and as Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson says, they will get the whole of the $25,000,000 of -common stock as a consideration for guar-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
anteeing the bonds of the Grand Trunk Facific Railway Company. The hon. the Minister of Justice has referred to section 11 of the Act of Incorporation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. By section 11 the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have the power to part with the stock for a consideration such as is mentioned in clause 3 of this Bill. I say it was perfectly idle for the hon. the Minister of Justice to make this statement that this $25,000,000 of common stock is to be sold for so many dollars. That $25,000,000 of stock passes out of the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and into the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company simply for the consideration that the Grand Trunk Railway Company endorses the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, just as has been stated by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson. As Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson says, it is hard to say what the prospective value of the stock may be, but the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be in a position to put one-half of that stock on the market at such a time as it deems advisable, realize the money on that stock and put it into the hands of the corporation. I submit that the amendment as moved by my hon. friend from Peel is a proper amendment, a wise amendment, an amendment in the interest of the people of this country, providing that before the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company enter into any agreement in regard to this $25,000,000 of stock the agreement shall be submitted for the approval of the Governor in Council. I think it is wise that that should be done. The hon. the Minister of Justice says that this is a domestic arrangement in regard to this stock, but it is a domestic arrangement which vitally affects the producers of this country. It is a domestic arrangement by which $45,000,000 of stock will become some day a burden, and a heavy burden, on the people of this country, because, some day they will be called upon to pay dividends on this stock and the producers of this country will have to furnish the money to pay these dividends.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to call the attention of the hon. the Minister of Justice to the answer that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson gives to the speech which he made just a moment ago. He contemplates nothing of what the hon. gentleman has stated here this afternoon. He tells a story to his shareholders directly the opposite of what the hon. gentleman has stated to be the condition this afternoon. This is what Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson said to Mr. Allen who had moved a resolution :
I will only take one instance of the inaccuracy of his criticisms. He boldly states that the liability upon the Grand Trunk will amount to nine millions sterling, and he divides that nine millions sterling into three millions liability in respect of guarantees, five millions

in respect of rolling stock, and one million in respect of the deposit. As regards the three millions of guarantee, that, as 1 stated to you, will undoubtedly he a liability, and, as I stated to you also, will swell the liability of the Grand Trunk Company. As regards the five millions for rolling stock, it is not five millions -it is estimated at three millions. With that the Grand Trunk has nothing to do. That rolling stock will he provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and. as the general manager will tell you, they have laid their plans for providing that rolling stock by a trust fund. Therefore, you may wipe it out and call it four millions. And as regards the one million deposit, that deposit will not cost you one single half penny.
Now I would ask the hon. Minister of Justice to reconcile the statement that he made a moment ago that the stock was required, first, to produce the deposit and next to provide for the rolling stock, with the statement of the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, who tells him that there is no particle of fact at the bottom of such statement. It is a very astonishing thing that he should make such a statement when the president of the Grand Tiunk Railway Company, whose case he is pleading this afternoon, tells him that he does not require the stock for any such purpose. The country will have some difficulty in reconciling the statement of a man who ought to know, a man who does know, a man, who, unless he is deceiving his shareholders, unless he is playiug a false part, is stating the matter correctly, with the statement of the Minister of Justice. The country will be able to understand the diffierence between the position taken by the hon. Minister of Justice and the position taken by the Grand Trunk Railway Company as announced through their president who knows the conditions, knows the plans, knows the relations between the two companies, knows how they are going to secure their rolling stock, knows how the deposit is to be put up and who tells us that their liability amounts to $15,000,000, practically, and that there is no liability beyond that. An hon. gentleman reminds me. that the $5,000,000 is merely held during the period of construction, and the Minister of Justice knows perfectly well that they have entered into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Company, in good faith I hope, to aid them by guaranteeing interim bonds during the period of construction. The government are going to finance the whole thing, and yet the Min ister of Justice says, that for the purpose of finding the money to provide for the interest on the portion of the bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company they need not sell these bonds. Bu* the Minister of Justice has not said that the Grand Trunk Railway may not. if they think proper, sell these bonds and put the money in their pockets. I leave the country to judge between the statements, made
by the Minister of Justice in his defence of the Grand Trunk Railway, and the statements of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, which aie exactly the opposite of what the Minister of Justice says.
