speechtext: I have as onerous a task, as I want in trying to perfect this contract and legislation, without assuming the defence of the Grand Trunk president. I hold no brief for that gentleman. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) says I do, and of course he never says anything that 'S not correct, and that he does not know of l.is own knowledge. However, so far as my own knowledge of my own affairs goes, I am of the opinion that I hold no brief for the president of the Grand Trunk Railway.
I did not say you did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know what the gentleman meant to say, hut I do know what he did say.
If the hon. gentlemau kept his ears open, he would know what I said.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not concerned with any statement made by- Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson. I will be judged, and the government will be judged, not by his statements, hut by this legislation. The construction which Sir Rivers-Wilson may put on the agreement does not add to, or take away one feather's weight from what the agreement itself says. If Sir Rivers-Wilson had in contemplation some of the things which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) said he had, that is his business, and he can carry out his intention if the contract permits him, but not otherwise. My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) said that the- intention of the government was to finance this enterprise pending construction The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) no doubt knows what the intention of the government is, and it may be I have not the same facilities for ascertaining it as he has, but in the meantime I have to consider the agreement. I cannot foresee what will be done ; I can only see what the agreement authorizes to be done.

I did not say the Minister of Justice held a brief for the Grand Trunk Railway; but I can tell him that he could not appear to greater advantage in their behalf if he were the solicitor for that company. His argument means that it would be unfair to the Grand Trunk to take any other view of this matter, than that which he entertains. Is the Minister of Justice not pleading their case ? The hon. gentleman denies and I believe he is right in denying that he is the advocate of the Grand Trunk Company. I did not say he was. but at the same time his speech has been a defence of the Grand Trunk and of the president of that company, and not a defence of the people of Canada.

The Minister of the Interior, in his speech on the motion to go into committee on these resolutions, assumed that some person had argued that the Grand Trunk Company would give away thirteen millions of the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which we said they would acquire for practically nothing. Upon being corrected upon that point he said :
The suggestion that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are going to make an enormous sum of money, is one that should have a moment's attention. There is $13,000,000 worth of common stock.
The hon. gentleman was minimizing it a good deal, because the Grand Trunk Company is to receive .$23.000,000, at least of the common stock, as declared by its president. He continues :
I have pointed out the obligations that the company have incurred. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, in the first place, have guaranteed the second mortgage bonds; they have entered into a contract which we are all familiar with in regard to traffic; they are bound to see that the working capital is provided, that the necessary betterments from time to time are furnished, and as against that they have $13,000,000 of stock which at the time is no value whatever.
I ask the Minister of Justice to point out, where the obligation is upon the Grand Trunk Company to provide the working capital and the necessary betterments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Except in so far as it is necessary for them to'provide it out of the twenty-five millions of stock they have to take over. Assuming that the $20,000,000 is altogether for the rolling stock, then there is nothing left except the $25,000,000 stock, and my argument and theory all through is: that the company having only the capital stock available, of course whatever money is available for the betterments of the road must come out of that capital stock.

The Minister of Justice has not met the point. This arrangement is very ingenious. We have the Grand Trunk Company which is to get the stock, as the president of the company has said, in consideration of certain support which they are to give to the Grand Trunk Pacific

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can quite understand some other hon. gentlemen arguing from the standpoint of what the president of the Grand Trunk has said, but I have a perfect right to ask my learned and honourable friend to argue it from the standpoint of the agreement.

I am perfectly willing to confine the argument to the terms of that agreement, and that is what I am doing. The position is. that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and others on behalf of the Grand Trunk Railway Company representing that company, will be making a bargain with Sir Mr. CLANCY.
Charles Rivers-Wilson and others acting as directors of, and representing the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson has told us, not only in his speech but in a carefully prepared circular to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company:
It should be mentioned that in consideration of the guarantees and other assistance given to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Railway are to receive the whole of the $25,000,000 common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
The other assistance to which he undoubtedly refers is the putting up of the deposit of $5,000,000 and with regard to that, (quoting again from the official report of the meeting of shareholders issued by the Grand Trunk Railway itself) ; he says :
As regards the one million deposit, that deposit will not cost you one single halfpenny.
And it is not costing a halfpenny, because, under the arrangement made with the government, interest is not demanded or received. What I come back to is this. There is a very ingenious arrangement. The Grand Trunk Railway Company does not enter into a contract at all. It creates tihe Grand Trunk Pacific Company, -autTlt guarantees certain bonds of that company and receives $25,000,000 of its common stock. The Minister of the Interior, speaking for the government and with all the authority of a minister of the Crown, has declared that it is the proper thing for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to receive, not as he says, $13,000,000 of Grand Trunk Pacific stock, but as he should have said, $25,000,000, and to make money out of it, because out of that money it will he obliged to do certain things, including the provision of the working capital and the necessary betterments. These are not idle words. They are the carefully considered words of a minister of the Crown speaking for the government, and I think we are entitled to know from the Minister of Justice what .the government, speaking through the Minister of the Interior, meant by those words. I find no such provision in the contract. Did the Minister of the Interior speak without the book ? It cannot be assumed that he intended to mislead parliament or the people of this country ; yet, If you cannot find something in the contract beyond what I have been able to discover, the language used by him is absolutely misleading. I would like to know from the Minister of Justice whether in all candour he is able to agree with the Minister of the Interior ; and, if so, will he point out the clause of the contract, or any clause of the statutes, which obliges the Grand Trunk Railway Company to do that which the Minister of the Interior said it is obliged to do ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only answer I can give to my hon. friend is this. It may appear to be a repetition of the same thing over and over again ; but I really cannot

state it otherwise. The common stock of the company is limited to $45,000,000. Assuming our construction of the contract to be the correct one, $20,000,000 of equipment is to be taken out of the common stock. That leaves $25,000,000. Under the agreement this must be taken over by the Grand Trunk Railway Company in order to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to carry out the purpose for which it is created-to provide money for the construction of the road, additional equipment, betterment, and so forth. If this stock is taken over by the Grand Trunk Company and the money is taken out of it for these purposes, -the money must, inferentialiy, come out of the Grand Trunk Company. That is the only explanation I can -give.
I,. BORDEN. My hon. friend must see that that is no explanation of the language of -the Minister of the Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may be a bad explanation, tout it is the best I can give.

I do not doubt that it is the best explanation my hon. friend can give ; but the Minister of the Interior distinctly said that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would be entitled to dispose of at least $13,000,000 of common stock and make what money it liked out of it, because it must have money in hand to perform certain obligations to be found in the contract. I say I cannot find these obligations in the contract, and no man in this House can find them. That speech of the Minister of the Interior was hailed as a remarkable defence of the financial portion of this scheme, and there are two or three arguments in it which will demand our attention before we get through. This was one of the most remarkable statements in it, and if the hon. Minister of Justice cannot give any explanation of it, I think we had better send for the Minister of the Interior and have his explanation. Unless you can find these obligations in the contract, and no man can find them, it was absolutely wrong for the Minister of the Interior to make that declaration to parliament and the country.
The argument of the Minister of the Interior merely supplements that of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson to the shareholders of his company. That gentleman said distinctly, in the circular from which I have quoted, that this stock was to be handed over to the Grand Trunk Company in consideration of the guarantee and other assistance given to the Pacific Company. The Minister of Justice accepts that, and justifies it on the ground that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is bound to make some provision out of that money. I say that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not bound to make any provision out of that money. But does not all this point to the necessity of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Peel ? What is the position ? I
mentioned it a moment ago. Certain gentlemen, acting as directors of the Grand Trunk Company are to make an agreement with themselves acting as directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, about a matter of vital interest to the people of Canada, and we are asking by this amendment that that agreement shall at least be made subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. We ask that because it has been declared by eminent authorities in this country, authorities respected by this government, that if that stock goes to the Grand Trunk Company for no consideration except the support afforded toy the guarantee and the making of this deposit afterwards, when the stock goes into the hands of bona fide holders who have paid ninety or one hundred cents on the dollar for it, it will be necessary to have the rates kept up to such a point as will enable them to receive dividends on that stock. There can be no question about that. Every dollar of bonds and every share of stock should be made available in cash as near the par value as possible. There is no doubt that such is the public interest. If this stock is disposed of for a mere nominal consideration such as the giving of a guarantee, are not the people of this country vitally interested in the raising of the rates which will be consequent on that ? When the Minister of Justice says this is a mere matter of domestic concern between the two companies, surely he forgets that very important consideration upon which stress has been laid, and upon which stress must be laid if we are to have any regard whatever to the rates which this company shall be entitled to ask from the Railway Commission in the future. Does not the Minister of Justice think that when such a mater is left to two companies who are controlled by the same body of directors, the government should have some supervision over the agreements they make as to the price at which stock shall pass from one to the other ? Is not that a reasonable proposition ? Can the Minister of Justice controvert it ? If not, will he not reconsider his position, and assent to the moderate and reasonable proposal of the hon. member for Peel ?

Let me give an illustration of what the leader of the opposition says. The Toronto Street Railway Company is capitalized at $6,000,000. The promoters of the company did not pay a dollar for that stock, and now the railway runs from five o'clock in the morning till twelve noon to pay dividends on that watered stock. In the afternoon the railway runs until five o'clock to pay the interest on the bonds that were issued for the construction. After that it runs on to midnight to pay thg., wages of the men. But the half of the day that street railway is running to pay interest on watered stock. If that watered

stock did not exist, tlie people could travel for lialf the fares they pay now, or the city's proportion of the earnings would be ever so much larger. It is a matter of vital interest that, if stock be issued, the proceeds should go to the railway. Otherwise an unnecessary tax will be put on the traffic. The traffic on every railway has to pay for the watered stock, bonds and everything else, and if the proceeds of any stock which is given out do not go into the railway, that only increases the charges which the traffic has to bear.
Mr.,R. L. BORDEN. I really think my hon. friend the Minister of Justice ought to show why some such amendment should not be inserted, inasmuch as the agreements relating to stock may prejudice the public interest. If the interests of the two companies alone were concerned, I would accede at once to the argument of my hon. friend, but he will not deny that the public interest is also at stake. I would ask him the question now, whether or not he contends that agreements between these two companies relating to the terms upon which the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific may be handed over to the Grand Trunk Railway, do not concern the public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In what respect will such an agreement affect the public interest to a larger extent than the agreement provided for in section 39 of the Railway Act, which may be made under similar conditions ?

That is probably the best answer which my hon. friend can give, but does he not realize that, as a matter of public policy that provision was struck out of the General Railway Act ? Why then should it be inserted in this special Act ? Why should this company receive any special advantage over other companies, as it will, inasmuch as the provision upon which my hon. friend relies has altogether disappeared from the general law of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not like to make the statement absolutely, but my recollection is that similar provisions to section 11 are to be found in other private Acts. I think that such a provision is in an Act passed this very session. Section 11, in its entirety, must be construed as meaning that the company is obliged to give out this stock either for cash or the equivalent of cash- for money's worth. There is a somewhat similar provision in the legislation of the United States. In England a joint stock company may pay out its stock in return for real estate to be used by the company itself, and the agreement which is made between the directors and the owners of the real estate, once it is put in writing, is conclusive between the parties. Similar legislation exists in the United States, but there the agreement is not conclusive. The whole matter is at large and may be investigated.

My argument is that section 11 provides that bona fide value must be given, either in cash or its equivalent, and that being the case, I do not see what the government has to do with the arrangement. Hon. gentlemen emphasize the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific is an enterprise in which the government is largely interested, but the government is largely interested in every railway built in Canada. True, the government guarantees the first issue of bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific and is liable for the interest during several years, but in other cases the government pays out large bonuses and subsidies, for which It gets absolutely nothing in return. Again, in connection with ordinary railway corporations, the public is interested as regards the question of rates.
I have looked carefully through the Railway Act and the decisions, and can find nothing which justifies the statement I hear constantly made that the stock is to be taken into account when rates are to be determined. There is no authority for that statement, but it probably has some basis, since it has been made by those who have given some consideration to the matter. 1 can find no justification for it, and should be glad to have some one give me a reference.

I do not think any one ever said it was to be found in an Act of parliament, but the authority for the statement is the Postmaster General and the exMinister of Railways (Mr. Blair), who always argued in that direction before the Railway Committee in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the limit of the authority.
It is not a very limited authority when we consider that the ex-Minister of Railways is chairman of the commission which is going to fix these very rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have to accept my hon. friend's statement, but I never heard of it before.
I have heard it again and again from the ex-Minister of Railways and from the Postmaster General. The Postmaster General is now in his place, and can state whether the reference to him is correct.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice takes this position. He says that this must be an agreement for va'lue. Well, that rather emphasizes the need for supervision by the Governor in Council. Who are to fix the values? The directors of the Grand Trunk Railway, on the one hand, and of the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other, and the former appoint and control the latter. You have these gentlemen meeting together and making an agreement. How can that agreement be questioned ? Will the Minister of Justice tell me who will question it ? I do not know of any principle at present which would justify any one

interfering, unless it would be some one interested in one or the other company. Perhaps the Minister of Justice can point out to me that the Attorney General of Canada might interfere. I would not think he could, but I have no strong opinion on that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Any shareholder or creditor.

Yes. That just brings us down to this, that no person representing the general public interest can interfere. But ought you not to have some person to represent the general public interest ? Is it not fair and reasonable that any such agreement, inasmuch as it may affect the rates, ought to be subject to the supervision of the Governor in Council ? I am sure my hon. friend, if he were not constrained by his position in defending the contract, would accede to the reasonableness and moderate character of this provision, t'Ut I appreciate the fact that he must defend this contract, and therefore must make out a case; but with all his ability and ingenuity it does not seem to me that he is making a strong defence against the amendment of my hon. friend. It is eminently reasonable that there should be some power representing the.people which would control in the public interest the terms of any such agreement.
I do not need to put it higher than that- it is an agreement which may affect the interests of the people of Canada. Because, when that agreement has once been made without supervision-I think the Minister of Justice and I are at one upon this point-it cannot be interfered with in the interest of the people of Canada ; it can only be interfered with at the instance of some one having an interest in one or the other of these companies And if you do seek to investigate, with what are you met ? You are bound to show before you can succeed that the agreement is not bona fide. How difficult it would be to prove that these directors were not acting in perfect good faith in making an agreement of that kind. It would be an almost impossible task. And so, any safeguard of that kind that we may have is really no safeguard at all. AVho could venture to say that the directors of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific might not think that this guarantee was perfectly good consideration for the stock, even though the opinion of the people of Canada might be that it was no consideration at all '!	*
Then after all, what is the objection to this amendment ? What objection should there be on the part of the Grand Trunk to having government supervision over an agreement of that kind ? And, even if they do object, why should the government, representing the people, object to undertaking supervision of that kind, which is absolutely in the public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With respect to the control of freight rates, has the attention of the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) been called to sections 39 and 19 ? Section 39 provides that the rates of toll to be levied are to be under the control of the Governor in Council of the Railway Commission. And section 19 provides that, lor the purpose of enabling the government tc determine the cost of construction of the railway or any portion thereof, or the cost cf the equipment supplied, or the net earnings of the railway of any part or parts thereof, the government shall have the right, from time to time, to appoint agents and investigate. Does not that put this corporation in a somewhat different position towards the government from the position occupied by the ordinary railway ? I offer that additional suggestion. I do not intend to be discourteous to hon. gentlemen on the other side, but really, when I have made my argument, I have done it to the best of my ability, and I do not see that anything is to be gained by repeating it. But in answer to the suggestion that it may be possible for the company, in consideration of the services rendered by the Grand Trunk Company, to hand over its stock for something less than the value of that stock, where are they going to get the money for the purposes for which they are incorporated, to create their terminals, to buy equipment, to provide all the things that their Act of incorporation says that they shall provide ? Where are they to get all this money, if their stock passes out of their hands without consideration ? Is not the capital stock provided by the Act necessary to raise means to carry on the purposes for which this incorporation is given ? The hon. leader of the opposition says they will get it out of the trust fund. Well, for instance, will they get out of the trust fund the money to make up the deficiency on the second issue of bonds ? Why. even the first issue, guaranteed by the government, will not yield par, and this second issue is not expected to yield more than eighty.
If my hon. friend would permit, me, I would say that so far as deficiency on the bonds is concerned. it would be made up by the issue of larger amounts of bonds. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no authority for it.
Why not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because the Act of incorporation limits the issue of $50,000 a mile for the mountain section and $20,000 a mile for the prairie section. And ns 1 understand it. the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite was that this was not

nearly enough to enable them to carry out the undertaking.
I never argued that

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that to have been the line of argument taken by lion, gentlemen on the other side.

The Minister of Justice has said that he knows of no authority to the effect that capital stock is to be taken into consideration in fixing the rates of transportation. I do not know what opinion the Minister of Justice has of hon. Mr. Blair, ex-Minister of Railways and Canals and at present chairman of the Railway Commission, but we know the opinion that the Prime Minister of this country has expressed, for he lauded that gentleman very highly as a most efficient and competent man, and a man of the greatest experience in railway matters. Now, we have the opinion of this chairman of the Railway Commission on the question of capital being-taken into consideration in fixing rates. Let me refer to this memorandum of the exMinister of Railway and Canals to that portion of it headed ' The promoters' rake-off ' :
The present disturbed state of public opinion with regard to railways and transportation arises from the feeling that tolls are excessive and discriminative. This feeling exists not only west of Lake Superior, but in Ontario as well. West of Lake Superior the great distance to ocean ports is a serious handicap, and any new transcontinental lines should he built under conditions which would make every dollar of bonds and every share of stock available in cash as near of face value as possible. If bonds may be disposed of by companies at a large discount, and stock distributed gratuitously, or on terms which produce little or no cash at all

That is what we have done. This $25,000,000 of stock is being issued not for the purpose of raising cash, but to give to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for guaranteeing these bonds.
-for construction and equipment purposes- which has been forbidden by law-the business such railways may do will, for dividend purposes, be always unduly burdened and will be a grave handicap for all time to the development of the interior.
With capital shares and bonds ultimately coming into the hands of innocent buyers at prices increasing with the growth of the railway traffic, it will be impossible for either the Railway Commission or the government itself to reduce tolls below a dividend paying basis. An appeal from the holders of the company's bonds and shares, to fixed tolls sufficiently high to insure a moderate dividend cannot easily be resisted, and as a consequence the country through its business and traffic is in effect as much charged, though Indirectly, with the weight of these obligations as if the amount was covered by an issue of government bonds.
Now, I would ask the Minister of Justice if he agrees with the statement of the exMinister of Railways and Canals which I Mr. FITZPATRICK.
have just read ? But this chairman of the Railway Commission and ex-Minister of Railways and Canals goes a little further. He says :
Moreover the system is not sound. Why should a few people be allowed to make themselves millionaires in such a way? No one now-a-days puts his money into the capital shares of a railway company at the inception of the undertaking. It has been done hitherto: it is not done now, and why not? Because with government assistance supplementing the sale of bonds the railroad can be built.
Just exactly what is being done in this case.
And yet capital shares are issued by the million and appear later, when the enterprise becomes a success, in the hands of the purchasers who clamour for dividends upon them.
Now, the Minister of Justice has stated repeatedly that this money was required for the purpose of buying rolling stock, providing terminals and so on. I would like to call his attention once more to the statement of the president of the Grand Trunk. He says :
As regards the five millions for rolling stock it is not five millions-it is estimated at three millions. With that the Brand 'trunk has nothing to do. That rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and, as the general manager will tt 11 you, they have laid their plans for providing that rolling stock by a trust fund. Therefore you may wipe it out, and call it four millions. And as regards the one million deposit, that deposit will not cost you one single halfpenny.
The Minister of Justice lays great stress on the five million deposit, which he said would be a burden on the Grand Trunk for which reason they will have to have the stock sold. I would like to get an expression from the Minister of Justice as to whether he agrees to the statement made by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, the present chairman of the Railway Commission.

The Minister of Justice quoted sections 19 and 39 as meeting the point respecting this $25,000,000 of common stock issued. Neither section 19 nor section 39 meet the point at all. Section 19 says :
For the purpose of enabling the government to determine the cost of construction of the said railway, or of any portion thereof, or the cost of the equipment supplied, or the net earnings of the railway, or of any part or parts thereof, pursuant to this agreement, the government shall have the right

and so on. That does not give the government the right to inquire into the value of what was given for this $25,000,000 of common stock handed over to the Grand Trunk; it does not give the government the slightest right and I challenge the Minister ol Justice to find under section 19 any such rights given. Then he also cites section 39 of this contract. The contract wou'd

aland on exactly tlie same footing if section 39 was not in at all, because section 39 provides for what is already in the general Act. Section 39 provides:
The rates and tolls to be levied and taken by the company upon any part of the said railway shall be under the control of the Governor in Council, or of such authority, commission or tribunal as is designated or constituted under any Act of the parliament of Canada for the regulation or control of the business of railways.
If that section were not there at all, this i ail way would be in exactly the same position as it is with this section. The hon. gentleman did not seem to consider the authority of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Blair) and the authority of the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) \ ery strong with respect to the common stock being taken into consideration when Ihe question of fixing the rates was being considered. I could quote for him authority that perhaps he would consider of some im-iortance, the authority of the right hon. the Prime Minister, who last session, when this was under consideration, took the same view and admitted as will be found in the debate of last session that this would have to be taken into account. I fail to see why it should not be taken into account. On what are you going to base your rates if not on the outstanding debt against the road, and surely the common stock must be taken into account ? The common stock can sell at par only because it is earning a dividend and the holders of that stock would have a right to come before the commission and be heard if the question of tjie fixing of rates was being considered. If the stock was purchased by them bona fide, and if the road was only capable of paying a fair dividend at the existing freight rates, then the persons applying to have the rates reduced would fail in their object and it is only reasonable they should fail. It is of extreme importance that the Grand Trunk Railway should have the power to obtain $25,000,000 of the common stock for what would have only a fictitious value, simply because they loaned the eiedit of their financial responsibility to the Grand Trunk Pacific in floating 'one-quarter of these bonds, necessary to complete the road. They are not under any greater responsibility after all than is the country, because the three-quarters and the one-quarter are placed together, and if the road was in liquidation the Grand I milk Railway would bear only their proportion of the loss and the country would have to bear three-quarters of the loss. Therefore I say that it is very important that this amendment should be accepted and I feel that it would if the government had at heart the interests of tiie people- and one would be sceptical of that when one stes how considerate they are of the interests of the Grand Trunk and how they
are losing sight of the manifest and plain rights of the people.

Let me point out why the government should protect the public interest in this case. Perhaps the Grand Trunk would not object to the government having the ratification of the agreement provided the present government were in power, but a government might come into office that knew not Joseph and then when the interpretation of this agreement came to be- passed on by the government there might be a government in office prepared to take the people's side of the question and to see that consideration was given for the stock. Therefore the Grand Trunk object to having the agreements between the two companies passed before the Governor in Council, and they have a real interest in having no such clause put into the Bill. It is in the interest of the public that this precaution should be included in the Bill. I cannot understand what objection the government can have for inserting an amendment that is absolutely in the public interest.

What the opposition proposes is that there should be an additional safeguard on behalf of the people. What the government objects to is that there shall be that supervision by the government which shall be for the benefit of the people. In the multitude of counsels on tiie other side of the House arises the great 'difficulty with which the opposition have from time to time to contend. At one time we have one line of action advocated by one minister and then we have an entirely different exposition made by some other minister. Take for instance the utterances of the Minister of Finance last session and contrast them with the statements of the Minister of Justice to-day. We cannot fail to be struck with the very complete right-about-face exhibited by the government. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R L. Borden) has been pointing out that we are dealing with a case where practically the same men will constitute the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The Minister of Justice does not seem to be impressed with the importance of that argument or to admit, as the leader of the opposition argues, that these two companies while nominally two companies are practically one company. Now during the whole discussion of this session we have had very prominently enunciated by the government, so far as they have spoken, the theory that we are dealing with two distinct companies. It is important to their position to-day, but it did not appear to be important to their position last session. The hon. Minister of Finance distinctly declared exactly what we contend to-day and what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has been contending this afternoon. At page 8571 of last

session's 1 Hansard ' the Hon. Minister Of Finance said :
It is a new company nominally, but the more you look into it, the more you see that it is one company.
That is what we say. There are nominally two companies, there is nominally a new company but the more we have looked into it, the more we have handled it and turned it over the more evident it has become that it is in reality one company, as the hon. Minister of Finance has said, and as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition lias said it will be the president of the one company dealing with the president of the other company, the manager of tthe one company,, dealing with and making bargains with the manager of the other company, and so the public will fail to have that protection which they should have, making it abundantly evident that the request of the opposition should be granted in the interest of the public.
I do not object

-says the hon. Minister of Finance
-to the statement made by- the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals when he said that these two companies were all ' the same red-headed boy.' We are rejoicing in the fact that these two companies are practically one, and that when we submit. this project to the people of Canada, we are not submitting a project of irresponsible promoters, but a project endorsed not only by the good will and pious resolve of the Grand Trunk

Whatever that may be. We have had the prayers of the right hon. the leader of the government and the pious resolve of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, whatever that is worth-
*-and pious resolve of the Grand Trunk, but the Grand Trunk put their guarantee and all their resources at the back of the undertaking of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
That makes it pretty evident that what has been contended on this side of the House Is true ; in fact, that this is one company and that is therefore the most cogent reason for requiring that when one branch of this company are dealing with another branch of this company there shall be some body to intervene on behalf of the people, and I think a most reasonable request is the request of the opposition embodied in the amendment which proposes to have the contract submitted to the Governor in Council. But, the hon. Minister of Justice says that sections 10 and 39 control the rates, and that even if there was something that we would not wish in regard to these stocks, still, the rates are controlled by these sections. We need not argue these sections any further. It is not a question of words. We have words, words, words in certain parts of the contract, but what has been pointed out Mr. LENNOX.
over and over again and what the ministry well know is that if you have watered stock and if you have this stock acquired by the Grand Trunk Railway Company for a nominal consideration, or for any consideration, and if this stock passes from their hands into the hands of bona fide holders you will have these people clamouring for dividends and in face of tbe fact that they paid 100 cents on the dollar or more for this stock you cannot by means of the Railway Commission or otherwise reduce the freight rates upon the railway. We have the hon. Minister of Finance discussing that branch of the subject as well and I will venture to read a few sentences from what he says in regard to that. But, before doing so let me say that in reference to the argument as to the Railway Commission controlling rates it was only the other day that we had a discussion in the House upon that subject. Is it not a notorious fact that only this spring the rates of the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been increased without application to the Railway Commission and that the same thing occurred last year ? Control is all very well in words but what yon want is effective control. If, Mr. Chairman, you will call it six o'clock I would rather not refer to this other matter before recess.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.

On section 2,

I have an amendment to offer to this clause. The clause now reads :
If any person has, in the period between the 15th day of March, 1904, and the date of the first of the certificates hereinbefore authorized to be issued, commenced to manufacture, use and sell in Canada the invention covered by the said ..patent; such person may continue to manufacture, use and sell such invention in as full and ample a manner as if this Act had not been passed.
Tlie word ' commenced ' is used in this clause. If some one had commenced illegally

to manufacture, even a day before the first date mentioned, he could continue to manufacture, although he commenced to do so in an illegal way. I also wish to provide for the case, for instance, of an employee of the E. A. Small Company who has been manufacturing during this period under the instructions and consent of the firm. My amendment is, that the following words.be added :

The Bill as printed covers the case of a man who commenced between these dates, but suppose he commenced to manufacture at any time before, even though he would be doing so illegally, the clause in the Bill would allow him to continue to manufacture. All I want is, that any one who might have been illegally manufacturing before that date should not be given any right he is not entitled to. If an employee of Small & Company has been, between these dates, manufacturing that article under their instructions and with their consent, we do not desire that this clause should give that employee power to continue to manufacture that article in spite of the patent.
This is to renew the patent.
Yes,
If a person acquired any rights previous to this being granted, you do not intend to take these rights away.

No ; not from the time the patent expired. But suppose he had commenced to manufacture before the patent had expired, he would be doing so illegally, and we do not wish to allow the person who 97
[ had been manufacturing illegally to continue.
That is after the patent lapsed.
Yes.
If he continues to manufacture after the expiry of the patent why should he not have the right ?

Let us suppose that previous to the lapsing of the patent some one had begun to infringe the patent; though it were only a day before the patent actually elapsed. The person fvho owned it, and whose legal rights became extinct on the lapse of the patent, would not be able to stop the infringement which had commenced previous to the lapse of the patent. 11 other words, we should not give encourag-ment to any one who has commenced illegally to manufacture this article. This is the common clause which I think is in all patent Bills which we have passed in this House.

Is the hon. gentleman sure that it is the common clause ? I do not think he will find the word 1 commencement ' in the common clause at all. If this man commenced to manufacture before the patent lapsed, the courts could stop him ; but if he commenced after the patent lapsed, he would be acting legally, and you would be taking away from him a right.

You are taking away a right that he has illegally obtained. This matter has been threshed out in this House on several ocasions. I have not had time to look up the different Bills which have passed ; but this' Bill contains exactly the same language as the Act which I have already quoted.
What is the effect upon a person who commences to manufacture a day after the patent lapses ?
The law as it stands allows him to continue to manufacture.

If the man who commences to manufacture the day after the patent lapses is allowed to continue, why should the person who commences to manufacture the day before the patent lapses be in a different position ?
All we ask is that if a man commences to manufacture illegally while the patent is in existence, he shall not be given exemption under the Bill.

I cannot see as a logical consequence why the man who commenced a day earlier should be in a worse position than the man who commenced a day later. He commences every day. Probably he would be liable to a penalty for manufacturing on the first day ; but otherwise I think he should be on the same basis as anybody else.

Because we protect the honest man who commenced to manufacture when lie had a right to do so, I do not think we should protect the dishonest man who commenced to manufacture when he had no
right to.	[DOT]
I do not think it follows that a man is dishonest because he commenced to manufacture a day before the patent lapsed. I do not see on what line the hon. gentleman is proceeding.
I do not think there is any objection to this provision from any source, and it is the usual practice in these Bills.

The directors of the company elected by the shareholders may make and issue as paid up stock, shares in the company, whether subscribed for or not, and they may allot and hand over in payment for plant, rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials of any kind, or as consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired, and also for the bona fide claims of contractors and engineers, such an amount of such common stock as shall he a fair and bona fide value for the property purchased.
His argument from that was that before they could issue that stock it must be shown that there was bona fide value given for it. The guarantee was not covered by the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of last year and this is simply an extension of those powers. The hon. They have to put $20,000,000 worth of rolling stock on the road, they have to build branches, they have to build a branch to Lake Superior, they have to build a branch to connect with North Bay, they have to build a branch to connect with Montreal, and they have to build a branch from Chipman to St. John. They are not bound to build these branches.

They are not bound to build them but the hon. Minister of Justice assumes that the $45,000,000 of stock would be required to do that. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have the right of issuing bonds to the extent of $30,000 a mile on every mile of the branch roads which they build to Lake Superior as well as to the other points which I have mentioned. Besides that in the province of Ontario they have a provisional subsidy of $2,000 in cash and 6,000 acres per mile. If it is the intention of the government of this country to subsidize any of the branch lines to connect with Lake Superior, North Bay, Montreal or the line between Chipman and St. John this House ought to know it. We ought to have the whole undertaking presented to us. We cannot understand the financial arrangements. The $45,000,000 worth of stock may not be sufficient and it may be more than is required. They will not require one single dollar of that stock for the purposes mentioned by the hon. Minister of Justice. Minister

Charles Rivers-Wilson to his shareholders is untrue and no gentleman like that would make a statement to his shareholders in England knowing it to be untrue. This is simply an extension of the powers granted under the Act which was passed last year for the purpose of allowing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company to enter into an agreement for the mere guaranteeing of the bonds. What bonds are they ? The only bonds that they can guarantee are those that are secured by a first mortgage on the road if the statement of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson is correct. The hon. Minister of Justice says that we are not bound by the statements of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, that we are only' bound by what is in the Act of parliament. Twenty-five million dollars worth of the stock was by the arrangement of last year to be given to the Grand Trunk Railway- Company for what reason ?-because they gave their sanction, virtually, to the enterprise. Because they guaranteed what were in the first place second-class bonds, but which are now first-class bonds ranking pari passu with government bonds. We ought to have from the railway department an estimate of the cost of the whole undertaking, how the money that is to be got from the people of this country is to be expended, what amount is to be expended upon the whole undertaking, what the whole undertaking involves and why they want this $45,000,000. Mr. Hays, the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway', said in his speech :
We expect to get assistance for these branch lines from the provincial and Dominion authorities. We ought to know that. Trunk which they can arrange for at any time within six months with the Bank of Montreal. Dear Sir.-I have received your letter of the 29th ult., containing copies of correspondence between yourself and the premier, and yourself and Mr. Griffiths, on the subject of the employment of aliens to the exclusion of Canadian citizens on the Grand Trunk Pacific surveys, dealt with in my communication to you of the 26th ult.

I also set forth |th'e names of eighteen persons in the company's service at the present time, all of whom are alleged to be American aliens.
I have again to request that the statements asked for in my previous letter be supplied at the earliest moment, and that in regard to the several persons named, an explanation he given as to whether or not they are American aliens, and if so, why, in each case, the appointment was made to the exclusion, if such he the fact, of Canadian citizens.
I notice in your letter to the premier, that it is stated that a very large percentage of the men employed on the Grand Trunk Pacific surveys are Canadians, and that only a small percentage are Americans. In this connection I beg to observe that it is not sufficient to show that a large percentage of the employees a're, Canadians or British subjects, for in the opinion of the government, in no instance should aliens, not being actual and bona fide residents of Canada, be employed to perform work' on the projected line, if it is possible to procure it being done by Canadians or bona fide re-' sidents of Canada.
I notice, also, that in the case of one or two Americans whose employment by the company is admitted, there is a statement indicating that they were engaged at points in this country. Whilst the employment of aliens by engagements entered into with them in this country may not technically constitute an infraction of the Alien Labour Act, yet it is substantially a disregard of the principle that the work, wherever possible, should go to British subjects, or to persons who are making Canada their home.	.
The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific is an undertaking of the first, national importance, and its national purpose should be kept constantly in view. It is to be expected that settlement and colonization will accompany the construction and development of the new road, and necessary work in connection with this construction should he used in every way to further this very desirable end. Nothing could more effectively defeat this purpose than the employment by the Grand Trunk Pacific of citizens of another country, whose interest in Canada is not an abiding one, and who may be expected to leave the country as soon as the occasion of their temporary employment is at an end.
I would again repeat the request that particulars asked for in my letter of the 26th ult., and repeated in this communication, he sup-I plied with the least possible delay.
Yours faithfully,
Minister of Labour.

This morning' I received the following letter from Mr. Hays :

My dear Sir,-On my return from a ten days' trip to the west I find your favours of May the 3rd and 9th in further reference to the complaints of Mr. Griffith on the alleged employment of aliens to the exclusion of Canadian citizens on the Grand Trunk Pacific surveys. I fear I cannot add to my letter of the 29th ultimo on this subject (in which I gave the names, nativity and occupation of all parties employed on our surveys) without at least taking some time to get the greater detailed information required. You will readily understand that since it is our practice to give Canadians the preference and employ others only when we cannot secure Canadians having the experience and ability considered requisite, we have not thought it necessary to keep a record in such detail as would enable us to give you off-hand the information you now desire, and as at present our men are widely scattered in the field, some of them miles off the line of railway, it will necessarily consume some time to comply with your request.
I may also say the same as to applications for positions, of which there have been a great many verbal and a great many written, some of both disposed of, to the satisfaction of the applicant, others declined without hesitation. These matters, as you will understand, are dealt with, not here at the general office by either the assistant chief engineer or myself personally, but by the division engineers who are responsible for their parties, employ the best men available and put them in the field, utilize them as long as they give satisfaction and dispense with their services when they cannot perform their duties properly.

Very truly yours,
(Sgd.) CHAS. M. HAYS.

It will be laid on the table no doubt.

ment to which we have just listened. But the notorious fact is that notwithstanding that the Canadian Society of Civil Engineers memoralized this government in January last and drew their attention to the fact that they were being turned down, that a preference was being given to aliens in a national work to be paid for by the people of Canada, absolutely nothing was done until April last, Until last month, although these surveys had been, going on for more than twelve months and specific allegations had been made again and again, and some of them had been read in this House giving particulars, giving the names in many cases, of these aliens. He must have known that the Alien Labour Law which we have on the statute-book was being violated because he and his colleagues were in communication with the Grand Trunk authorities for months in connection with this project. He must have known that they were employing large numbers of men and sending out surveying parties over the projected route. Was it not his duty to see that the men employed, especially when the government paid for the work, were Canadians or British subjects. He has done absolutely nothing except to write some two or three letters to the Grand Trunk. I am in the sense of this committee when I say that instead of writing these letters asking Mr. Hays and some other officials of the Grand Trunk whether the allegations made by Canadian engineers were true or not, he was in duty bound to send some officer of his department-and X think there are sufficient officers employed to enable him to send one for this purpose-up to the west, whence these complaints emanated, and to have obtained for himself, for his own satisfaction, information on the ground as to whether these complaints were well founded or not. Is it satisfactory to be told after numerous complaints extending over a period of several months, that the minister himself is not satisfied with the replies he has received from Mr. Hays ? Is it not his bounden duty now to send some officer from
the Department of Labour to investigate these complaints ? In matters of much less consequence, when the Labour Department was in its infancy, officials were sent here and there throughout the country to make reports ; but now, in a matter of vital and national importance, when complaint after complaint has been filed by Canadian engineers who are out of employment, nothing has been done except to write two or three letters to Mr. Hays and to be insulted by Mr. Hays by not having replies made and not having the in-fomation sent to him as it should have been sent. On March 22nd last I got a communication in connection with this matter :

It is just as the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) said. If Canadians are employed, they are chain men and axe men.
These aliens are employed, not because the Grand Trunk Pacific cannot get Canadian engineers capable of filling the positions, but because the manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific is himself an American, and is now showing his leaning for his native land by employing engineers from the United States, and thereby keeping Canadian engineers from getting employment to which they are entitled

The above remarks apply with equal force to. the western division between Winnipeg and the Pacific.
If this railroad is to be built we ask that Canadian and British engineers be employed. Neither the Great Northern, Northern Pacific Railway or other lines in the United States will employ a Canadian or British engineer unless and until he becomes a naturalized citizen of the United States, and not even then unless he has a family and has established his home there, and it is common knowledge that Canadians have been repeatedly deported from the United States to Canada.
The Acts in force in the States bordering on Canada forbid the employment of any person in an official capacity unless he is a citizen of the United States by any municipality, corporation, railroad company, or state authorities. ' The Lucin cut-off crossing over Great Salt lake, Utah, is still giving trouble. No statement of the difficulties encountered in this work has yet been given out by the railway officials.'

Yet the man who superintended this work is appointed chief superintendent of construction on the Grand Trunk Pa-oific Railway, while we have a number of Canadians available who have forgotten more than Mr. Burt is ever likely to know about railway construction, and his appointment is a gross insult to every Canadian and Canadian engineer.
