His animus towards Canadians was thus clearly defined at the outset. The most recent and flagrant exhibition,of this was ignoring the professional civil engineering element of Canada, and his establishment of United States aliens upon the entire survey of the Grand Trunk Pacific from coast to coast, and the absolute exclusion of Canadians, thus placing this survey in the hands of men who are entirely unacquainted with the topography, climatic conditions, and general natural features of the country in which they were operating. The majority are men of entirely immature and inexperienced judgment, who were given Mr. CLARKE.
this work to the exclusion of Canadians of mature judgment and experience. These aliens receive much higher remuneration, and the construction of the work being otherwise enormously augmented in cost through their said inexperience, and we would impress upon the government that they should not be stampeded into any acceptance of said plans or surveys until the work has been carefully gone over and thoroughly revised by Canadian engineers under the immediate supervision and control of the government.
We cannot too strongly impress upon the government that, this may mean an enormous saving of expenditure in cost of construction and maintenance, saving of grades, structures and curvature, and the possibility incidentally of a considerable saving in mileage.
It should also be borne in mind that the vast financial interests associated with the Transcontinental Railway lines of the United States are liable to do what they can indirectly to degrade the efficiency of a new Transcontinental line, and the government will do well to guard against the surreptitious influences which, are now at work and will be continually at work to accomplish their object in making a dangerous rival less dangerous by in every possible way decreasing its efficiency.
We would respectfully invite the attention of the government to the items concerning alien labour incorporated by the Ontario government in the specifications and contract of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, and also, we believe, made effective by Act of Ontario legislature. We would strongly urge similar legislation and executive action upon the part of the Dominion government in all its dealings in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific and in all its relationships of that work to the interests and well being of the Canadian people.
As an illustration of the gross waste of public money now going on from coast to coast through ignorance of the country and its topography by the aliens now engaged on the Grand Trunk Pacific we will mention the following:-
The great prairies extending westward from Winnipeg to the foot hills of the Rocky mountain bear evidence of having once been an immense inland sea, with its several beaches marking the successive levels of the waters of what geologists have been pleased to term the great post glacier Lake Agassiz. Between Winnipeg and Edmonton there are two lifts of about 550 feet each, which serve to divide the prairie country into three great subdivisions having the same general characteristics. The first prairie steppe includes the low plain of Manitoba and is bounded on the west by the first lift of 550 feet, which is simply a series of benches or terraces forming the so-called Riding, Duck, Porcupine and Pasqual mountains.
In some places these terraces form a precipitous escarpment, and the only route for a line of railway is by one of the valleys cut through the escarpment by the rivers, or the sand dunes in front of the escarpment. It is by means of these sand dunes that the Canadian Pacific Railway is carried from the first to the second prairie steppe. The difficulty is increased by the fact that the Assiniboine river before reaching the plain of Manitoba runs through the second prairie steppe parallel with the escarpment or lift on the western boundary of Manitoba, and in so doing has scoured out a valley about 300 feet deep and from one to two

miles wide, the river 300 feet wide following a tortuous course along the floor of the valley. Therefore a railway line after rising 550 feet from the first to the second prairie steppe, has to again drop down 300 feet into the Assiniboine valley and rise 300 feet on the opposite side.
Literally almost every foot of the escarpment and the Assiniboine valley for 40 miles north and 40 miles south of the proposed location of the Grand Trunk Pacific has been surveyed over and over again since the year 1875 by the engineering parties working under Sir Sandford Fleming, Marcus Smith, Walter Moberly and many other well known Canadian engineers and in later years by the Canadian Pacific Railway, Manitoba and Northwestern Railway Great Northwest Central Railway, Canadian Northern Railway, &c. If a Canadian engineer had been in charge of the Winnipeg division of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, from his personal knowledge of the country he could have laid out at comparatively small cost the only available routes, but the American in charge of this work, through ignorance of the topography of the country or of the work already done by the Dominion government and other railway companies, has had for months one complete American survey party and at times two American survey parties in the field floundering all over the country trying to find a line through the escarpment at a cost of at least $12,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, with no progress yet made, except that they are the laughing stock of the engineers throughout the west. In fact the reports sent to Montreal by those bright specimens of American engineering have been alrflost en-tireiy copied by a stenographer from the works y Professor Macoun, Dominion government explorer, and others in the Winnipeg library and not from their own personal knowledge or experience.
That is the communication which accompanied the letter sent to the Minister of Labour on 2nd of April, six weeks ago* and I want to draw the attention of the committee to this fact : that while the Minister of Labour sent this communication to the Grand Trunk Railway officials at once and asked them if these statements were correct, the engineers who made the complaint and who volunteered to send a deputation to wait upon the government to substantiate their allegations, had no notice whatever taken of their request, although the Grand Trunk were asked for information as to the accuracy of these statements, the men who made the complaint declare at page 7 of this communication :
A deputation of Western Railroad engineers of good reputation, if permission be given, will be only too glad to wait upon the government! a+n+ -give fuI*er details and prove the facts
If the Minister of Labour had accepted that suggestion, if he had invited the men who made the complaints to come down here, he could have heard their statements himself; and having heard their statements, lie would have been in a position to judge of the value to be placed upon them; or, fail, ing to invite them down here, he might have sent some of the officials of his own depart-9S
meut up to the west who, by interviews and conversations with these men, could put the department ill a position to be much better informed than it apparently is to-day.
Mr. Griffith, the secretary, is in the city at the present time, brought down here at the expense of the government.
I am very glad to hear that. Might I ask the Minister of Labour when he came here ?
I do not know what day he arrived here. I telegraphed him if he would come down I would pay his fare, or expenses, or something to that effect.
Was that after the hon. gentleman had written twice to Mr. Hays ?
And I got an answer from him saying that he would be here on Wednesday night, or this morning. He appeared this morning.

I am glad to hear that the Minister of Labour, at the end of six weeks, has asked Mr. Griffith to come down here. The letter to which I have referred was written on the 2nd of April. The minister has acknowledged that he received that letter. It asked that a deputation of engineers be allowed to come down here and substantiate these statements. But now, the hon. gentleman, having failed to get any information from Mr. Hays, having been flouted and ignored by the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway, telegraphs to Mr. Griffith to come down, and he says Mr. Griffith is in the city to-day. I congratulate him on bringing Mr. Griffith down after six weeks of delay. But if Mr. Griffith was actuated by the motive which Mr. Hays alleges in making these complaints, would it not have been as well to have had Mr. Griffith and a deputation of these engineers brought down at the same time, so that the government would have been placed in communication with more than one man, especially as that man had been discharged by the company ? I leave the hon. gentleman to make the necessary explanations of what I consider to he gross laxity in connection with this whole business. On the 8th of April Mr. Griffith addressed a letter to myself, in which he said :
We have written three letters to the Minister of Labour, sending in the names of twenty men, as a first instalment, all American aliens, engineers and draughtsmen, employed east and west of Winnipeg.
Actually east of Winnipeg, where the Canadian people have to assume the entire responsibility and expense in connection with the construction of the road-
I am given to understand that in all probability a great effort will be made by the' Grand Trunk Pacific Company to discredit our statements. We therefore beg respectfully to

ask that you will force this matter of alien labour,to the attention of the government, for if they deny our charges the Minister of Labour has the evidence right there.
As an instance of the manner ^ in which the engineering positions are filled in every division of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the following statement may be used by you in the House : the division engineer at Winnipeg, G. A. Kyle, has appointed his brother, M. Kyle, his nephew, Raymond Heckman, and a brother-inlaw locating engineers on his division. None of these men are in the opinion of Canadian engineers competent for the positions to which they have been appointed.
I am sorry that I have been compelled to take up so mueli of the time of tjie committee in referring to this matter. If the Department of Labour had been equal to the occasion, if the Minister of Labour had given that prompt personal attention to this matter that its importance deserved, we should not need to be discussing the condition of things that exists at the present time. I think I am in . the sense of the committee when I say that there has been gross neglect of the interests of our Canadian and British engineers and surveyors. They had a right to expect sympathetic treatment from the men who are commencing the work of construction of this great transcontinental road. They had some right to be considered by the Grand Trunk authorities as well as by the Minister of Labour. But after these surveys have been going on for a long time, and notwithstanding tlie fact that the government was notified in January last by the Canadian Society of Civil Engineers, and since then again and again by Canadian engineers in the west, and although emphatic protests have been made against the treatment dealt out by these Grand Trunk officials to Canadian professional men, we find at the end of all this time that the Minister of Labour thinks he has discharged his duty by reading to us copies of two or three letters which he has sent to Mr. Hays, expressing his conviction that this great national work must be carried on in a truly national spirit, and that thei'e must be no dlscriimlnation against Canadians in the work of the surveys. May I appeal to the lion, minister that there is yet time to do something that will benefit the Canadian engineers and surveyors in connection with this work ? If the hon. gentleman desires to listen to the appeals which these men have made, it is not yet too late tor him to despatch an officer to Winnipeg to make inquiries himself into the situation and advise the minister whether these statements are well founded or not. If they are not well founded, it is not fair to Mr. Hays and the Grand Trunk officials that they should be iterated and reiterated, as they have been for months past. If they are well founded, the Labour Department has shown itself in this case not to be equal to the occasion or worthy of the confidence of the wage-earners of Canada, who look to it Mr. CLARKE.
for protection when flagrant violations of th j law are brought to its attention.

Before the minister replies, I would like him to tell us whether iir. Griffith states how many aliens hav [DOT] been brought in ? Mr. Hays, in writing to the premier, stated that 96 per cent of the employees on the surveys are Canauians. What is Mr. Griffith's reply to that ?

Perhaps the statements of Mr. Griffith and Mr. Hays wall not tally. The fact that their statements are contradictions of each other wilt not advance the issue much. Mr. Griffith gave me a list in the various letters of some twenty-two. I collected them and set them forth in a communication to Mr. Hays. I am glad that my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), at tills late stage in his political career, is developing such a sympathy with the wage-earners of Canada. This is not his first appearance in public life; he has grown, almost, old in the service. He ' has been selected by the public, and particularly by the wage-earners of Canada, for various public positions during a quarter of a century, and during all that time until the last eight years, while his political allies were in power in Ottawa
They were not building the Grand Trunk Pacific.

They were building the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the hon. gentleman was never tired boasting of it ; and yet the first thing done on the completion of that railway was to put an American citizen at the head of it, to be' enriched at tlie hands of hon. gentlemen op posite, to be succeeded in turn by another of the same nationality, and from that day to this the hon. gentleman has never ceased paying homage to those same distinguished men.
Did the hon. gentleman not help to secure him a knighthood, and did he not join in offering him a seat in the Senate ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was long after he became a Canadian. He was not a Canadian when you employed him.

My hon. friend has not forgotten, perhaps, that prior to this government coming to office, this country was the favourite stamping ground of the aliens, who took the plums that ought to have been kept for Canadians only. When did the hon. gentleman ever rise a voice on behalf of the Canadian people ?
When the hon. gentleman is in a position to do something, he is doing nothing.
Will the hon. gentleman have patience a moment and I will deal with him ?
May I ask a question ? At the time lie refers to, had the Americans an iniquitous labour law as they have to-day ?

The question is, what should be done with Canadian public money ? Does the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) say that if the Americans were to wipe out their law, we would go back to the same state of affairs as existed formerly ?
Did not my hon. friend say that our law was a retaliatory law ?

I said that that was the origion of it. I said that retaliation was what led to its establishment, but I went on to add that I considered that our law, if weak, should go further, and if necessary go beyond the American Act, and I say so to-day. The hon. gentleman is manifesting great zeal this evening for the workingmen. But for twenty-five years he never raised his voice in public to assist them. He is a man who has always been ready to make his living out of them.
Shame.

I am speaking of his public career. Several times he has been enabled, as commissioner, to earn public money, and is therefore one to whom the workingmen should be entitled to look to specially for consideration. What has he to say now with regard to this particular question ? He .tells us that he has been in correspondence with Mr. Griflith a long time. He has read letters, which he had in his possession long be'fore this question came to my attention. This matter was first drawn to my attention by Mr. Griflith, in his communication dated the 2nd of April, and received by me some time subsequent to that date. Prior to that, correspondence had been carried on with various ministers but not with me.

He ignored you altogether. Sir WILLIAM MULOCK. I do not see why he ignored me. but he chose to write to other ministers. Ultimately, however, I received a communication from him and then took up the matter. My first communication was in the early part of April, and since then I have endeavoured to get at the facts. My hon. friend complains of delay. Did he receive any correspondence from anybody giving him information prior to my receiving any ?
I read the correspondence.
The hon. gentleman read letters which he said he received in March.
The 22nd, I think.

What has he been doing since the 22nd of March ? Why 981
did he not bring this matter to the attention of the House long ago ? Long before I was seized with the matter, he had his information, and yet he remained asleep. He did not even take the trouble, on behalf of the wage-earners to raise his voice when the grievance was brought to his attention but remained tongue tied until the leader of the opposition mentioned the matter and until the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) gave notice of legislation and a motion as well. It is only to-night, on the 13th of May, nearly two months after he got his first information, he rises to take part in the debate. Had he been so zealous as he pretends, he would have brought the matter up in the House at a much earlier period. What has he been doing during the seven or eight weeks that have elapsed since he got his first information ? Has he no duties to perform in the interests of the wage-earner ? If he is their special chosen advocate, why has he not been doing his duty ? He has very little to do except to attend to such matters, yet this particular case did not interest him sufficiently to induce him to make the slightest reference to it until to-night, when the debate is on and he could not very well shirk it. Yet this is the gentleman \Vho has elected himself the special advocate of the wage-earners of Canada. I do not sympathize with Mr. Hays in this matter. On the contrary, all my sympathies are the other way. I believe in the enforcement of the law in every reasonable manner, so that people resident in Canada will receive the benefit of employment to be paid for by the public money of Canada, if they are fit for the work ; and until it can be shown that there is not sufficient labour in Canada of the right quality, the presumption is that we are quite equal ourselves to perform all the public works for which our people have to pay. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says I should have sent a man to the west to make inquiries. What sort of a wild goose chase would that have been ? Where would the man have gone ? Would he have got any more information by going to the offices of the Grand Trunk Pacific at Winnipeg ? Could he not be deceived there and misled just as well as down east ? Or was lie to go into the prairies or the mountains rnd see these men and try and ascertain from them where they were born, their [DOT] nationality and how they came to be employed ? No. I think the proper course was to go to headquarters, to the responsible head of the Grand Trunk Railway, and get from him the information. If he should fail to give us that information, there is a way by which we can reach him. I submit, with all respect, that there has not been that great delay of which my hon. friend complains. I received my first communication some time in the first week of April. That referred me to some correspondence which had been sent to Ottawa. I had to collect

that correspondence from the different departments, and I immediately followed that up by writing, in the first place, to the secretary of the company. The hon. gentleman says I wrote to some irresponsible. I wrote to Mr. Wainwright. Does the hon. gentleman say that he is an irresponsible ? He is an official of the Grand Trunk Kailway of long standing.
Did you get an answer ?
I did not receive the answer I ought to have got.
Did you receive an answer at all ?

I do not think I did, giving the information I desired. I wrote to the right person in the first instance ; and if he delayed or neglected to answer, that is not my fault. I should like to know to whom my hon. friend would have me write. Mr. Wainwright is one of the leading officials, authorized to receive correspondence with the Grand Trunk Railway. At all events, he was written to on the 19th of April, and a further letter was sent Mr. Hays on the 26th of April. After a few days, the answer came Mr. Hays was out of 'Canada, and would be back and send an answer towards the latter part of the week. That letter reached me this morning. That is the first letter I had from Mr. Hays, except the one I spoke of, in which he said he had written to the premier, and I have again put myself on record with him. Now I venture to say that my action has been much more speedy than that of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). He tells us that he l-eceived a letter on this subject in March-that he was informed of these doings then. To whom did he write ? Did he write to the Grand Trunk ? Did he write to the government ? Did he exercise his undoubted right to stand up in this House and at once call the attention of the House and of the government to the facts ? Did he in the slightest degree attempt to discharge his duties as a member of this House with respect to this very Important subject-the employment of aliens on a public work ? I fail to see that however zealous he may be in debate be has manifested that sincere interest in the sub. ject that would have resulted, had he been moved by it, in effective action. Now', we are only at the threshold of this great subject, the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I suppose that in due time the Grand Trunk Pacific-this I only reason upon ; I have no information on the point -if they are making surveys of this eastern division, which is to be constructed by the government, may ask us to pay for those surveys. It is probable they have that in their mind, though I do not know' it. But if they make such a request it will be a question then whether any disbursement in respect of wages or salaries paid to aliens Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
under the circumstances under discussion should be recognized. Up to this moment, at all events, the government have not disbursed public moneys in these surveys, thej have not recognized these surveys. The government are not parties to the surveys m any way, up to this moment no public money has gone into them, and perhaps uo public money will go into them, or, at all events, that portion of them which may he performed by American labour. That is a question, of course, for future consideration.
Did not the Prime Minister say last year, and also this year, that he would pay for these surveys ?
I do not know what the Prime Minister said on that subject last year or this year.
The Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) is in his place ; and, if I am not mistaken, he made that statement last year.

speechtext:
No, I did not say .that.
I said that the Grand Trunk had entered upon these surveys of their own motion, and, if the surveys were found to he useful to the government, and were approved by our chief engineer, whoever he might he, I saw no reason why they should not he bought and paid for. But there was no agreement on the subject.
Mr. iSAM. HUGHES. I happen to have it here. It will be found at page 14646 of 1 Hansard ' of last year :
I see by tile Montreal ' Star ' of this evening that Mr. Hays says he has survey parties all over the road. Is the government paying for these?

No arrangement has been made with respect to that. But if the Grand Trunk have made surveys which can he properly utilized, I think we should he glad to have the work advanced to that extent and to utilize the result. And if we utilize the work of the surveys, no doubt some arrangement will be made to hear our fair share of the expense.
It would be n question of what would be our fair share, if we were called upon to pay for work performed by aliens under these circumstances.
I understood that they were to pay their share east of Winnipeg and the others their share west of Winnipeg.

I do not know of any understanding between the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific, aud the government on this subject. The Finance Minister says there is no understanding. Whatever the government do hereafter will he entirely voluntary on their part. But, Mr. Chairman, it is only a preliminary feature of a great work, that is the construction of the Grand Trunk Pa-I cific. And the amount of work involved
309?

in these surveys is not very large as compared with the total work to be performed in this construction of this great enterprise from ocean to ocean. And, even if the debate is acute, and if hon. gentlemen manifest a keen interest in this matter, for my part, I derive a great deal of satisfaction, from that fact. My hon. friends are welcome to any point they suppose they can make against me, whether I have been astute and active as they would have been under the circumstances or not. If t have not come up to the previous expectation of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) then, judging from the record of that hon. gentleman on this matter, how far would he fall, under similar circumstances, below the standard he now sets up. But, Sir, I say that I do not regret-on the contrary I am gratified by it- the attention that is being given to this subject, because it means that steps must be taken, by legislation or otherwise, to put this question on a more satisfactory basis, one that will make it clear to the Grand Trunk and to all concerned that it is the policy of the Canadian people to have the work, if possible, performed by the Canadian people themselves. The subject, therefore, will be productive of excellent results if it is educational in the way I have mentioned. I do not think, at this stage, with only part of the file read, we could enter with any satisfaction into a controversy as to where the truth lies. If it should turn out that the truth is on the side of Mr. Hays, then we shall have been unjustly commenting upon him. I am not one to undervalue the statement of Mr. Griffith simply because he may have ceased to be an employee of the Grand Trunk. Quite the contrary ; it has nothing to do with his credibility. I had the pleasure of meeting him for the first time this morning. I formed a high opinion of him. As to his professional qualifications, he showed me testimonials that indicate that he is an engineer of eminent standing, reliable
Trying to smooth him over a bit ?

No, I have nothing to smooth over. I simply desire to get at the truth, by the examination of Mr. Griffith, Mr. Hays, or anybody else. I say that at the present moment the question of fact is to be determined and it seems to me only fair to endeavour to get each party to make their statements, and. if they do not harmonize, to appoint some independent tribunal to inquire into the facts, so that we may know where we stand in regard to the controversy.

I am sorry the Minister of Labour (Sir William Muloclc) did not attempt to answer the allegations that have been made against him by men for some
of whom he expresses much appreciation, Mr. Griffith being one of them. I am sorry he did not attempt to give some explanation of his gross and unpardonable neglect in looking after the interests of these men. He is the head of the department that was organized especially to give attention to the grievances of the toilers, and to protect those who feel themselves aggrieved by the infringement of the Alien Labour Law. I read to the hon. gentleman the correspondence I had received and read it in the most respectful way. And the answer is a tirade of abuse-I suppose that is the best, in fact the only answer the hon. gentleman could have made- a tirade of abuse in which He charges me with making a living out of the working classes-
No, I did not intend that
That I was making a living out of the working classes-
No, I did not say that. No

If the hon. gentleman is prepared to take it back, of course, T must accept his apology. I have never had the honour to serve the working classes in any official capacity in my life, except as a representative of the people, and then not specially as the representative of the working classes. But I have felt it a great privilege, as well as my bounden duty, in this House or in any other assembly where I had a voice or vote, to give that vote and raise that voice in their behalf. It is because I felt it in line with my duty as a representative of an industrial constituency that I am trying to stir up the hon. gentleman to make his actions square with his professions at the present time. What under Heaven is the use of having a Labour Department if the Labour Department does nothing ? In January last and again in March and again in April the hon. gentleman and his colleagues received statements accusing the Grand Trunk Pacific of employing aliens and refusing to employ Canadians. One would have thought, as there is some Irish blood in his veins, that when he had been turned down and treated in such a contemptuous way. his letters to Mr. Wainwright and Mr. Hays not being answered, he would have been stirred up to do something. When I asked him why he had not sent some one to investigate, he asked me : What would have been the use

Send where ?
Mr. CLARKE-of sending some one on a wild goose chase. He has brought one gentleman down by telegraph. Is that a wild goose chase on which he is bringing Mr. Griffith down ?
Send where ?

To the city of Winnipeg whence emanated the complaints which were brought to the attention of the minister again and again but which he has overlooked and neglected. He said he thought this matter should not have been discussed until the correspondence had been completed.
I did not say so.
I am in the judgment of the committee-

I did not say so.
Mr. CLARKE-when I say that the hon. gentleman suggested to the House that the debate, should be postponed-

No.
Mr. CLARKE-until the correspondence had been completed. ' Hansard ' will show what he said.

What I said was that I did not think that this issue could be determined by a partial reference to the correspondence nor could in fact the merits of the issue be dealt with by the correspondence until we found out whether the different parties agreed Or differed. At present we have charges made by Mr. Griffiths, and I cannot say we have distinct denials, and yet we cannot say there are sufficient admissions made by Mr. Hays. At present therefore the record is not in a complete enough state to determine the merits of the point in. issue.

The hon. gentleman might have thought of this before he got up to make a speech of nearly an hour's duration in the effort to put the best possible face he could on his lack of interest in this matter and his failure to do something in this matter. Why did he commence to read the correspondence ?
Because the leader of the opposition-

The leader of the opposition did not suggest that it should be read; but before the correspondence was read he drew attention to the fact that he had made a motion for all this correspondence but that it had not been brought down. In his zeail to cover his tracks and to try to make the working people of Canada believe that something had been done, the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock), brings down the correspondence, including a letter received this morning from Mr. Hays and the answer he sent to-day to Mr. Hays, showing how earnest he is in the interest of the Canadian workingmen, surveyors and engineers. He writes letters to Mr. Hays and Mr. Hays answers by writing a confidential letter to the premier, but the etiquette which exists in the circle in which Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
he moves would not permit him to let the Canadian people know what the contents of that letter were. To-night he brings down that partially completed correspondence. What for ? To try if possible to put a good face on the grossest instance of neglect that has ever taken place in connection with the administration of a public department in this country-
Dear me !

Failing to make as good a case as he hoped to make, he thinks it is in keeping with his dignity and with the very high position he occupies to abuse those who are advocating that Canadian labour should not be discriminated against at least in this great Canadian national undertaking, and he asks me what have I been doing since I received these communications ? On March 21, I brought this matter to the attention of the House before I had received any complaints at all, and I have referred to the matter twice since then. If the hon. gentleman had looked up ' Hansard,' he would have found that out, and also that the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) had brought this matter, to the attention of the House twice, so that since March 21 this very question has been before parliament five times, and notwithstanding that fact what did the minister do ? If we were neglecting our duty in only bringing this matter before the House five times since the 21st of March, what has he been doing since the matter was first brought to the attention of the government? Does he think that because he has written two or three letters, intended for publication, to Mr. Hays, declaring that Canadians must not be discriminated against, that that will be an atonement for the neglect which has characterized his department since this matter was brought to his attention? Does he think the working people, the surveyors and the engineers will be satisfied with such a lame excuse, or that the vomiting of abuse on myself and other hon. gentlemen who speak on this matter will be considered as a sufficient answer to the statements we have made face to face and have given him an opportunity of denying since the allegations against the Grand Trunk Pacific were made. He telegraphed for a man to come down here and substantiate them. On the 13th of May he tells us that Mr. Griffith is here, and he regards that as a discharge of ail the obligations on himself in this matter, and as a sufficient atonement for his lack of energy and lack of zeal in investigating the statements. I have brought this matter before him three times. The first reference was on March 21. I did not receive the first communication until March 22nd. 2.	This relates to the Department of Labour.
3.	It is the intention of the government, in its new agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to provide for the employment of British subjects as surveyors and engineers, in the work of surveying and construction of the new Transcontinental Railway?
3. The matter is under consideration.
speakername: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals):

speakeroldname: Hon. JAS. SUTHERLAND (Minister of Public Works).
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY-ALIENS AS SURVEYORS.
speechtext:
In the absence of the Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock) I would answer question No. 2, as follows: It is not the practice of the government to issue general instructions respecting deportations, but to deal with each case as it arises.
That is the answer to the second question. The hon. gentleman's colleague saddled the hon. the Minister of Labour on March 28, with the responsibility of dealing with this matter, and when in respectful language we ask him whether he has or has not dealt with it, he charges us witli being neglectful of our duty in not bringing it to the attention of the House. On the 28th of March his attention was brought to it, and one of his colleagues said : ' It is in the Department of Labour.' He seems to think he has discharged his duty by writing letters to Mr. Wainwright and Mr. Hays. '
The gentlemen who made the complaints offered to come down and make good their allegations before the Minister of Labour. It never suggested itself to the hon. gentleman that it was the proper thing to do in view of this serious state op affairs, in view of the fact that Canadian surveyors and engineers were being ignored, and he never thought it worth his while since the 28th March or the 2nd of April to get further information in respect to this matter from the men who made these charges. But I brought this matter up again, as will be seen by reference to page 080 of ' Hansard.'

1.	Has the Minister of Labour received any communication from Mr. George L. Griffith, of Winnipeg, provincial Secretary for Manitoba of the Dominion of Canada Institute of Amalgamated Engineers, calling attention to the number of aliens employed on the surveys of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and giving the names of aliens employed in connection with such work at Winnipeg and Edmonton?
2.	When was such communication received?
3.	Is it the intention of the government to take action upon Mr. Griffith's communication, and to order the deportation of the aliens complained of?

1.	Yes.
2.	One received on April 6th, and two to-day.
3.	The Alien Labour Act, as amended, contains provisions entitling any private citizen to bring an action for alleged violation of the Act, and on a conviction being secured, the government would be prepared to direct deportation. The law does not authorize the government to bring such action.
Three times since my attention was drawn to this matter I have brought it to the attention of the hon. Minister of Labour, and although I did so I am charged with gross neglect of my duty, while the hon. gentleman plumes himself upon having discharged his duty. He has had this matter before himself and his colleagues since January last, and he has allowed Mr. Wainwright and Mr. Hays to insult him by neglecting the ordinary courtesy of even acknowledging the communications which he sent to them about it. I am willing that the artisans of the constituency I represent should be the arbiters between us as to whether I have not tried to serve them and serve Canadian engineers and surveyors by at least drawing the attention of the government to the charges they have made and by demanding that these charges should bt investigated and justice done to them in preference to the aliens who are being brought into this country. The responsibility does not rest on my shoulders of enforcing the Alien Labour Law. It rests primarily and fully upon the shoulders if the hon. Minister of Labour ; and squirm as he may, and explain as he may, the men who have been aggrieved, and who have felt themselves aggrieved, will place the responsibility upon the right shoulders. I a in perfectly satisfied as to that.

Mr. Chairman, I am quite prepared to accept any responsibility devolving upon me in the matter. I am quite satisfied to place my record alongside that of the hon. gentleman on this subject. The hon. gentleman has said that I have abused him. I think I began ir. deference to the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition who, before six , o'clock, made an inquiry in regard to the

subject, and I thought it proper to let him know the substance of the correspondence as far as it indicated the intentions of the government. I did not have any idea that I was in the first instance to be honoured by such a reception as the hon. member for West Toronto gave me. He says 1 abused him. Pray, if I abused him, what did he do to me before that ? I might complain of his having begun it and I would ask him to-morrow to read the choice and cultured language in which he charged me with the grossest neglect and in which he assailed me with the most unqualified abuse. Then, he complains that I should point out any of his own shortcomings. I think that what he is indignant at is that he finds that the government has got upon solid ground and is taking the proper position and he finds most of his political capital somewhat destroyed. If I had the correspondence here, which, I understand has been sent to the ' Hansard ' room, I think I could read a few passages from the letters that have given him so much worry and which have so disturbed his peace of mind this evening. He says that they were written for publication. Pray what is his speech delivered for ? Does he expect that it will never be heard of outside ?
I was trying to stir up the minister.

That is a very desirable thing to do if the minister is in need of it. In my judgment before inviting a large number of persons, a delegation or otherwise, to come to Ottawa or elsewhere to determine the rights and wrongs of this question, the first step is to ascertain what the parties to the issue themselves think and say about it. The representative of the engineers says one thing and we are desirous of ascertaining what the representative of the company says in reply. If Mr. Hays were to admit the whole case it would be unnecessary to bring witnesses from Winnipeg specially to hear their evidence, nor would it be common sense to send men scouring this country to use up the taxpayers' money in a useless effort. My hon. friend wants us to spend money in a useless way to pretend to do something instead of really doing something. We are not here to engage in such work ; we are here to do business. If to-morrow the Grand Trunk Railway Company admit that these statements are correct, we do not need to send witnesses all over Canada to find out whether they are correct or not, we do not need to bring delegations to Ottawa to prove them and to ascertain where we stand.

Is it the practice of the Department of Labour, when charges thal aliens have been brought into the country have been made, to write to the parties interested to ascertain whether the inform-Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
ation is correct, as was done in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific ?

I cannot say whether it is the invariable practice. These matters are conducted departmentally to a large extent, but in a case of this kind, when the matten was brought to my attention, it seemed a very proper thing, that, before attempting to deport these men, we should inquire into the facts. That inquiry is only a means to an end and that must be the deportation of these men if they have violated the law. It would be a high handed procedure for the attorney general of Canada to arrest a large number oi men, take them to the frontier and expel them from the country unless he had the security that the law' affords. Thereto e, he should be reasonably sure of his ground before interfering with people in this country. It is the part of prudence. If, for example, we had seized these men, sent officers all over Canada to find them and when found sent them out of the country, what would have been the consequences? It would be a serious matter to arrest a lot of foreigners and to send them out of the country unless we were justified by the law. It would not only be an outrage upon these individuals but it-might involve us in complications of a very serious character. It is well enough for the hon. gentleman to say that we should rush ia and take a step of that kind. The hon. gentleman said he was not responsible. Now, I quite agree with him, that, from Ids remarks, he is not responsible. He is asking us to do these rush things without observing proper prudence. That would not be the course that any responsible gov-ei nment ought to pursue. We have a duty tc perform, we have responsibility and he would be the first one to criticise us if we had not in the hist instance taken a reasonable procedure such as that which we have adopted. We are now getting into close quarters with the Grand Trunk ; they will not be much longer able to evade the distinct issue or admission, and we will then know what the next step is.

It seems to me that if the government had not been in pretty close quarters with the Grand Trunk, these men would have been deported long ago. This is not a new question : it was brought up last session by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes). The attention of the government was directed to the subject or ought to have been directed to the subject through the Department of Labour, by resolutions which were passed ac a meeting of engineers held in the city of Montreal in the latter part of January last. At least five times during the present session the attention of the government has been brought to this matter. What has been the result ? The result has been, that the

Grand Trunk Railway have been humbugging the government for the last six weeks.
For the last six months.

1 will only go as far back as six weeks. The Minister of Labour talks about being cautious. Why, I have the names here-the Minister of Labour has read them-of some 20 or 22 men whose residences in the United States were given to the government six weeks ago, and all that has been done by the government since, is to write letters to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to which they received either no answers or very evasive and indefinite answers. The Minister of Labour thinks this the most extraordinary diligence on the part of the government in a matter of so great importance to our people. I understand that it has been represented to the government that 90 per cent of the engineers, transitmen, topographers, draftsmen, chaiumen, and picket men, are American citizens. I don't know whether that statement is true or not, but it has been so represented to the government as far back as the 18th of April, nearly a month ago, and not one thing has been done except to write some letters to the Grand Trunk Company, to which no answers, or merely evasive answers have been given. I understand that the Minister of Labour promises an investigation by commission. I imagine we may expect to receive a report from that commission about the time these surveys shall have been completed, and then, of course, it will be exceedingly comforting for these men to know, after the work has been finished, that the representations made to the government when the work commenced have turned out to be absolutely correct. The situation is aggravated by the fact that surveys are being made by the Grand Trunk Pacific, not only on that portion of the line which they are to build, but on that portion of the line which the government is to build. The government is not only permitting the law to be transgressed on the western division, but it is permitting the Grand Trunk Railway to evade the law with regard to surveys on the eastern division, and these surveys, according to a statement made by the government this session, may be adopted by the government and paid for by them if they proved satisfactory. The public money of * this country, spent in building a railway owned by the government. is to be given to American citizens in defiance of our own alien labour law. That is the actual situation. One would think that when the government commits the making of these surveys to the company it would stipulate-without the question being raised in parliament at all-that these surveys should be made by Canadians. One would think that the Department of Labour
would not require to be galvanized into activity under conditions of that kind.
They promised to give us a national road built by Canadian engineers.
I think he will be disappointed.

He will not be disappointed unless the government manifests a greater diligence and activity in the future than it has exercised during the past two months. The names and addresses of these aliens are here; they have been in the hands of the government since the 10th of April. When these names were submitted to the Grand Trunk Railway, is there any reason why that company could not answer in twenty-four hours, whether or not these men are in their employ and whether they are aliens ? Here are the names :

G. M. Kyle, engineer, residence, 1320 North Yorkima Ave., Tacoma. Wash.

-	Kellar, engineer, residence, Cleveland, Ohio.

William Meyers, engineer, residence, Portland, Oregon.
-	Nutting, locating engineer, residence, Oregon, United States.
W. Mason, draughtsman, residence, Tacoma, United States.
M. H. Goodman, draughtsman, (now transferred to Grand Trunk Pacific Office, Montreal).
-	Van Arsdaile, divisional engineer,, residence. Portland. Oregon.
-	McNeil, district engineer, residence, Indiana.
W. Jones, engineer, residence, St. Paul, Minnesota.
-	Hare, engineer, residence, Wisconsin.

Stopple St., Cincinnati, Ohio.

W. Mann, jr., engineer, residence 1215 Stopple St., Cincinnati, Ohio.
-	Hicks, transitman, residence, Tacoma, Washington.
-	Anderson, topographer, residence, Seattle, Washington.
The Minister of Labour lias these names as I understand.
I have sent them off.

He lias sent them off to Mr. Hays. I want to know why Mr. Hays, or other proper officer of the Grand Trunk Company could not tell this government within twenty-four hours whether or not these men are in their employ. Are not these men on the pay lists in Montreal or cannot the information be procured by telegram?
You can get every one of them in the audit office.

The information could have been procured and would have been procured if the Grand Trunk Railway Company had not seen fit to trifle with the government and to humbug the government, and if the government had not permitted itself, for what reason I do not know, to be trifled with and humbugged. What was the reason that the Minister of Labour did not issue a pre-emptory message to the Grand Trunk Railway Company demanding an answer to liis letter at once, when he saw. as be must have seen that he was being trifled with.
The Grand Trunk would dismiss the government if he did.

The Minister of Labour may take that suggestion into consideration. It is not my suggestion, but the suggestion of my bon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes), and it is much in the line of what has been told us by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs, that they were obliged to concede the amendments in this Bill to the Grand Trunk Company because otherwise the Grand Trunk Company would not go on with the undertaking. I suppose that it may with equal reason be said by the government; we must permit the Grand Trunk to humbug us with regard to this matter, because if we press them too closely they may not go on with this undertaking. I join with my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) in trusting that even at this date the government will do something-
Hear, hear. Get busy.

After having conducted a sufficient amount of polite correspondence, which eventually might be inserted in some guide to polite letter writing, it would be just as well if the government would really do something. There is a statute of the land that can be enforced.

The Minister of Labour says to-night that the next step would be deportation. He was not of that opinion on the 11th of April, when he gave his answer :
The Alien Labour Act, as amended, contains provisions entitling any private citizen to brine an action for alleged violation of the Act, and on conviction being secured, the government would be prepared to direct deportation. The law does not authorize the government to bring such action.
We do not know exactly which view of the law to take. But if the law does not contain a provision permitting the government to take action, it is because an amendment to that effect which was introduced by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) was voted down by the government, if my memory correctly serves me ; and if the government is helpless because it cannot take action, it is helpless because it did not see fit to insert in the statute the provisions necessary to enable it to act. In any case the government should have some control over the Grand Trunk Pacific Company in respect to a matter like this ; and when names and residences and particulars sufficient to enable the government to act and to put pressure on the Grand Trunk Company have been in its hands for a month or six weeks, it does seem extraordinary that the Minister of Labour should see fit to present to the House such an absolutely bald and insufficient explanation as he has presented to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon.' leader of the opposition attempted to strengthen his position by reading an extract from an address by a professor in an American university, it is hardly to be expected that these gentlemen across the line can pay sufficient attention to our affairs to know the changes that have taken place here. That professor evidently thinks the conditions are the same to-day as they were when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, and he naturally assumes that as a large number of Americans were brought in at that time to enjoy the money which the people of Canada contributed, therefore the same condition of things exists to-day. We shall have to take pains to let bur American friends know that a great change has come over the affairs of Canada, and that the interests of the working classes are protected now as they were not in former times. The hon. leader of the opposition, in his opening remarks, made what was evidently a slip when he said that the government had committed to the Grand Trunk Company the surveys east of Winnipeg. He must be aware that the government never committed these surveys to the Grand Trunk Company or made any arrangement about them. The Grand Trunk Company entered upon these surveys and sent its survey parties into the field before it had made the contract with us. These survey parties have continued

to work, and It would be a fair subject for consideration whether these surveys, if found suitable for the government railway, should not be taken over and paid for at a fair price. If not approved of by the engineer chosen by the government to superintend the construction of the railroad, then I take for granted that they will not be paid for. I do not think there has been any such delay in this important matter as some lion, gentlemen opposite suggest. It is true, there was general talk months ago about some Americans being employed on these surveys. During the recess I had a conversation with Mr. Hays on the subject, and he denied the allegation, declaring that all or nearly all who were employed on the work were Canadians or British subjects. Up to that date we had nothing before us but general reports. It was only recently that we had reports giving the names of Americans who were alleged to be employed. Until these names were received, I do not see how the matter could have been investigated. The hon. leader of the opposition read a list of names under date of the 16th of April. Well, this is the 13th of May. It is not a dreadfully long time ; and in the meantime what other course could the government have pursued except to write a series of letters to the Grand Trunk officials ? Hon. gentlemen opposite talk of that as if it was an unreasonable and improper course. I say it was the proper and reasonable course. Whatever steps are taken may not be taken entirely under the Alien Labour law. The Grand Trunk Company might be acting entirely within the limits of the Alien Labour Law and yet be pursuing a course to which this government would object. They might engage Americans in Canada, and thereby escape the provision of the Alien Labour Law, and we would not agree to that. It might be proper occasionally to bring in a man for some special duty or who had some special skill ; but that would only occur'in rare cases, and I would not quarrel with the Grand Trunk Company about it. When we had the statement of Mr. Hays that fully 96 per cent of the engineering staff engaged on these surveys were Canadians or British subjects, and up to that time we had no specific allegations of names, there was not much to investigate. There has been in the last few weeks in the hands of the government a list of names of alleged Americans employed on these surveys; and I do not see how the government could have proceeded in any better way than to call the attention of the Grand Trunk Company to these specific allegations and ask for a prompt reply. Owing to the absence of Mr. Hays-that is the excuse given-his reply has been delayed. I agree that there should have been a more prompt reply. The hon. leader of the opposition says that there should have been a reply within twenty-four hours, stating whether these men were employed on the road or not. Yes, that reply
could have been got within twenty-four hours ; but the question was not whether they were employed, but whether they were Americans. The mere fact that they were employed, and that they resided in such and such a place, would not be conclusive proof that they were Americans. It would constitute a prima facie case that would demand an inquiry ; and it would not be unreasonable that Mr. Hays should have a moderate amount of time to communicate with his officials in the west, and ascertain whether the allegation was correct on not.

The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour have referred to the Grand Trunk Railway engineers as being Americans. Let me tell them that the Canadian Pacific Railway engineer was a Scotchman, Mr. James Ross.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman not know that the chief engineer who resigned last week, Mr. McHenry, was an American ?
He was not the chief engineer of the Canadian Pacific Railway under construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He has been the chief engineer of the Canadian Pacific Railway for several years past.

Not under construction.' I would like the hon. gentleman to name an American engineer brought in at that time. There was no alien labour law in the United States at that time, and no need of any retaliatory spirit on the part of Canadians. This matter was up last session. I brought it to the attention of the Minister of Finance, when he introduced the $500,000 vote for the National Transcontinental Railway. He said it was intended to send out survey parties. Mr. Monk asked when would the work of survey begin, and the Minister of Finance replied that the work would be arranged by section and begun as soon as surveyors could be appointed. He added :
There is every disposition to push the work. I should think that immediately after the session parties will he put in the field and the work proceeded with as long as the season will permit.
I then drew attention to what appeared in the Montreal ' Star,' and quoted the paragraph as follows :

Hays, general manager and second vice-president of the Grand Trunk Railway, has made the following statement regarding the company's plan for completing the Grand Trunk Pacific:-
The reconnaissance survey is proceeding vigorously, and in fact has been ever since early last spring. We have between fifteen and twenty parties in the field, some of whom have about completed the work of their division. Others will keep on all through the winter.
On some portions of the route, where the country is comparatively unknqwn, for instance.

in the Lake Nepigon district, owing to the lack of transportation facilities, supplies are difficult to obtain and progress is not as great as otherwise might be the case.
I merely mentioned that to show they were at work east as well as west of Winnipeg. Then I concluded :
So it would seem that the Grand Trunk Pacific are surveying the land to the north. This is a nice little piece of campaign literature, and I thought I would read It for the benefit of the Minister.
On which side?

Weil, turn it either way. What I want to know is whether the government will, instruct the chief engineer, when they appoint him, to take over these survey parties. I understand that they are almost entirely American.

We have no arrangement with the Grand Trunk in that respect. I understand their surveys are between North Bay and Winnipeg. Of course, only that part of their line which coincides with the contemplated line of the government can be used. But if bona fide surveys have been made, which are found useful for the government's purposes, I think we should take them over and make a fair allowance for them.
Then I interposed the question :	' And
take over the engineers, too ? ' To whicn the Minister of Finance replied : ' Not necessarily, but take over the surveys.' Last year I distinctly made the point that these were American engineers. The Minister of Finance must know that all Mr. Hays has to do is to ask his auditor, and in five minutes he can get the name of every man cn the survey party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What about their nationality ? That is the question.

He can quickly find that out. Where there is a will there is a way, but the fact of the matter is the government has to do just exactly as the Grand Trunk Railway dictates. That stands out clearly. The government are powerless, and the House and the country are quite aware of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has afforded us another illustration of the idea on his side that the old time still continues. That is a mistake. After the close of last session, in consequence of various statements, including that which the hon. gentleman himself made, about the employment of American engineers, I wrote to Mr. Hays and received from him the positive statement that there was no foundation for these charges. My hon. friend from Victoria says he pointed out that the engineers were Americans, but he did not mention any names. We had on the one side newspaper reports that these were Americans, and on the other we had the positive denial of Mr Hays, who stated that, with the exception of a very small percentage, they were Canadians and British subjects.
You would not expect the hon. member for Victoria to send you photo graphs. He gave you the names.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did not give any names.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not at all. All he did
was to make the general statement that they were Americans. He said that everybody knew they were. Well, everybody did not, and we do not know it even yet. I have the statement of Mr. Hays-and whether we all agree with him or not, we must admit that his word is entitled to some respect-I have his word, and he assures me that these reports were erroneous, and that with few exceptions the engineering staff was composed of British subjects. Recently, however, when specific charges were made and the names given, the matter assumed a uew aspect, and there has been no unreasonable delay since.

When Mr. Hays states that the staff is 96 per cent Canadian, he is simply humbugging the government. The staff would include the polemen, the bottle-washers, axemen, Indians and wagon drivers, and these the company will pick up; along the line wherever they could get them. But it is no secret to any one, except the ministers, that the head men are Americans, and that is recognized from one end of the country to the other.

I had a motion on the order paper which I intended discussing after the papers were brought down, but for some reason or other some of these papers have been presented this evening. It seems to me that the question which should concern us now is what remedy we should apply to get rid of an evil that all parties seem to agree is. existing. I consider that some of our friends in the opposition have gone to very extreme lengths in attacking the Minister of Labour. It seems to me that he has made a very straightforward statement, and that the correspondence shows he is thoroughly sincere in the matter. I would like to remind some of tho hon. gentlemen in the opposition, particularly the hon. member for Pictou, who has been endorsing the attacks on the minister, that there is no corporation of this country which has imported so many aliens into Canada as the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that there is no provision made against the importation of aliens. At the same time I approve entirely of the position taken by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). I agree with him that it is a most serious grievance that in a great enterprise such as this, men should be brought from abroad and put into the best positions. It is the duty of the government, not to enter into correspondence, but to enact legislation

which will remove this grievance. If the correspondence with the Grand Trunk Railway proves anything, it proves that the company have not much regard for the opinion of this House.
Of the ministers.

No, of members. What is necessary is for this parliament to pass legislation which will make that impossible. There should be some provision in the agreement compelling the company to employ Canadians, or some general legislation enacted which will make it impossible for public bodies, who receive Dominion assistance, to employ people outside of Canada. I have been thinking of this myself for some time. If the hon. members of the opposition were sincere, they would support tion enacted which will make it impossible for any public enterprise, supported by public money, to employ other than Canadian labour. Of course, there may be conditions which render it necessary to bring in exceptional men from the outside.
I have no desire to throw any obstacle in the way of an, enterprise. I conceive that sometimes it may be necessary to bring in people from outside into Canada. In fact, I know of instances in the coal mining operations of Vancouver Island when it was imperative to have men brought from the other side to operate certain machinery which was made in the United States and not made in Canada, and which had not been operated in coal mines previously. So, I can easily conceive that circumstances may arise repeatedly when a small number of men require to be brought from the other side or from the old country. But I contend that a public enterprise which is supported by the money of this country should be carried on under the condition that the working men of this country should get the work of that enterprise. Let any man in this House put himself in the position of an engineer in the city of Winnipeg with a wife and family, depending upon his profession for a livelihood and paying the taxes which contribute to the remuneration of this company, and finding himself set aside and denied employment in order that a place may be given to an American. That is the position, and we ought to recognize this as important. I would support the principle, and I hope the House will support the principle, of making the general provision that, wherever assistance of Canadian money is given either to individuals or to companies in this country, Canadian workmen shall have the preference on those works. The Grand Trunk Pacific authorities, I believe, are anxious to employ Americans. I think there is every indication that that is then-disposition. I think there is every indication that the Canadian Pacific Railway has always wanted to employ Americans. We can .turn to the press of only a short time
ago and see that the Canadian Pacific Railway were making contracts on the other side to bring in labour from that country into Canada. There is the evil, and we all recognize it. Let us get down to the remedy ; and the remedy is to pass legislation in this parliament to provide that, when Canadian money is spent for either individuals or companies, Canadian workmen shall have the preference.

I would like to say just a word to contrast the action of the United States in matters of this kind With our own. In the expenditure of the harbours and rivers appropriations, and on all works receiving government assistance, they are not even entrusted to the ordinary American engineers, but engineers of the United States navy or the United States army have superintendence of these works. But we in Canada do not even require that our own engineers shall be employed, but we allow the big companies to import scores of aliens to the detriment of our own men.

I think that the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) in suggesting that we should have wider powers to prevent this evil should have suggested also that we had better provide a minister to enforce them. The difficulty is not so much in the direction the hon. gentleman has endeavoured to prove, but it is with the government. We find the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) having a friendly chat with the Grand Trunk officials

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wrote a letter.
Yes, a delightful letter such ast the minister might be expected to write. But I venture to say the officer did not answer the letter except in conversation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think Ihe correspondence will show that he answered it politely.

That was last October, seven months ago, and the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) slept all the time -knew nothing about the matter. The duty of the Labour Department, the moment a question of that kind comes before its notice even through the newspapers, is to institute an inquiry. But we have the unhappy admission from the Minister of Finance that he had some communication with Mr. Hays and Mr. Hays made a denial. Now, Mr. Hays occupies a prominent and responsible position, and his word should be worth something. But his word is not worth so much that he alone is to be heard. The hon. gentleman takes the denial of Mr. Hays, a most respectable man, without inquiry into the other side of the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no other side at that time-no names mentioned.

Does that strengthen the hon. minister's position V Was it necessary to give names? The hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) called attention to it. The hon. minister was not concerned whether they were American engineers or not, but only gave consideration to the question whether the surveys would be taken over and paid for. The other ques-tiou he ignored and did not even discuss it. The hon. Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) wrote letters, but those to whom they were addressed did not think it worth while even to acknowledge the receipt of them. I ask the Postmaster General if he thinks now that he was treated with courtesy or with the dignity that should characterize the head of an important department, to have Mr. Hays, or any person else write to the Prime Minister with regard to a question that belonged entirely to his own department, instead of writing to him (Sir William Mulock). Was not that a form of evasion on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of the very question presented to them ? Borden) has pointed out, the Minister of Labour might have learned within two hours sufficient at least to have known how much there was in the accusation made by these gentlemen who had made representations to the government on the subject and showed that a certain number of Americans, whose names were given, had replaced Canadians. What does that mean ? The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) has stated that the disposition of the Grand Trunk Pacific authorities was to employ American labour. How easy it is to find a pretext against another, as the wolf did against the lamb in the fable. him. The minister, I think, has shown that he was, perhaps not intentionally, but criminally careless. The government have been helpless, existing by the grace of the people who are over them. This corporation hold them in the hollow of their hand. That it as clear as the sun at noon-day. and proper idea of the resources and future of this country. The government hope that Mr. Hays will make this all right. That is absolutely clear. It is pitiable, it is absolutely contemptible and yet the so-called representative of labour weakly attempts to back them up in that business.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman has found great fault with what I have said. He has said that 1 favoured general legislation. If general legislation were embodied in an Act that covered all these companies, surely that would be legislation in the interest of the labouring men of this country. The hon. gentleman is anxious to secure the adoption of special legislation for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, but afraid of general legislation that would operate against his friends. That is the position that the hon. gentleman takes. I stated that general legislation ought to be enacted so as to make it impossible for others than Canadians to be employed by all companies in this country which are receiving public money. But, tile hon. gentleman, in his anxiety, is only able to say something about the Grand Trunk Pacific. He does not wTant the Canadian Pacific Railway to be interfered with. He only wants to interfere with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to which he is opposed. ! do not think that the hon. gentleman was quite fair to me in his remarks in view of the fact that I stated plainly that I considered that it was the duty of the government to provide a remedy for these grievances. I did not shelter myself under the nmberella of the government. I stated emphatically that it was the duty of the government to remedy these grievances. I never heard the hon. gentleman make a statement as plainly as that against his own party. I do not think it is possible for the hon. gentleman to take as independent a position as that in regard to his own party, and I think the hon. gentleman's slight presence in this House ought to make him more careful in undertaking to criticise those who are defending the rights of labour by their presence in this House. I want to say that I was elected as an independent supporter of all measures affecting the labour unions of this country and I appeal to this House if, on every labour question that has been before the house, I have not taken an independent stand. On the national policy, I am Liberal in contradistinction to those who support that policy, and nobody knows it better than

the hon. gentleman. Nobody knows better than he that the Liberals of the constituency which I have the honour to represent supported me and elected me and that the labour men had confidence that I wyould support them upon any question affecting their interests which came up in this House and they are going to do it again. I did not shelter myself behind the government, but I said that it was the duty of the government to provide a remedy for these giev-r.nces.

The hon. gentleman has been so short a time ir this House that he has ventured to refer to the slight presence of myself in this chamber. I have been for 21 years in this House and I venture the prophecy, that, although I am going out of it, the hon. gentleman will go out of it with me and he has not been 21 years in this House yet.

I may say that this case now before the committee is one almost parallel to the condition that prevailed down in Cape Breton in connection with the iron and steel company. Very soon after the American management took hold of it it uvas ouite recognized that Canadian labourers were no longer wanted. We saw in fact from 50 to 75 Americans placed in positions there to the exclusion of Canadian professional men, Canadian mechanics and Canadiau labourers. I wish to point out to the committee that my colleague and myself made representations about 18 months ago to the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier), to the hon. Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) and to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and we were present when a meeting was held by the members of the government and the members of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. We placed our case before them there with the result that the right hon. Prime Minister of this country gave bis ultimatum to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and intimated that the concern had to be Cana-dianized, with the result that within two or ihree weeks an exodus of Americans from Sydney began and I am in a position to say to-night, that not a single one of these men who was brought over by the Americau management is now in his position in Sydney. I only took on that, as I am going to take on this, a fair independent position, and

that Is that in connection with the expenditure of public money, either in the shape ot bonuses, or, I am going to go further and say that in cases where high protection is awarded to industries in this country I am going, as far as I can as a public iran, to insist that the government shall look, not only after the interests of the plutocrats who invest their money, but shall also look after the interests of the men who sweat blood to sustain their interests. 1 simply take my seat with the expression of my belief, knowing as I do several ministers in this government, that effective measures will be taken immediately to meet the condition that we are now discussing.

Admitting that there is a grievance in this connection ; we have heard what the lion. Minister of Labour proposes to do about it. May we know what is the proposition of our hon. friends on the other side ? I think the hon. member for West Toronto was very explicit in his assertions. Will he be kind enough to inform the committee what he proposes to do 1

If the hon. gentleman will turn to ' Hansard ' of 1901, when the present Alien Labour Act was being amended at the instigation of the right hon. the Prime Minister, he can make himself acquainted with what my views were as to a proper Alien Labour Law. I have sent away the books, but it is hardly [DOT] worth while ascertaining whether the hon. gentleman voted in favour of my amendments or not. But I submit that an effective mode would have been provided if the amendments that I suggested in 1901, when the present Alien Labour Law was being put on the statute-book, had been adopted. If the hon. gentleman wishes to know what my view of the present situation is I will tell him that if I were Minister of Labour I would take immediate steps to verify the allegations which have been made by the engineers in Winnipeg, and if I found the allegations were sustained I would insist upon having the aliens employed by the Grand Trunk dismissed at once, and their places given to competent Canadians.
The hon. gentleman has answered my question so well

No ; you answered it too well to be logical. It is possible to overdo even a good thing, and when the hon. gentleman said that his position in the first place was that the Alien Labour Law should have been made so and so to be effective, I could understand that. understand that, but I cannot understand the one position set over against the other

v Mr. OLIVER. The hon. gentleman is responsible for that when he submits a contradiction of terms to the House. I will have to wait until the hon. gentleman reads my remarks in ' Hansard ' and has an opportunity of thinking them over.
