I must confess that that argument is a brain twister to me. At this early hour in the morning I will not inflict another speech on the House, but I would suggest that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver} read the ' Hansard ' of 1901 for enlightenment as to the reason why the Alien Labour Law is in its present condition.

If the hon. gentleman cannot understand it must be attributed to the brain tangling effect of his long and able speech. I am not here as a representative of labour, but if I were I would look askance at the arguments that are put forward to-night as alleged in the interests of labour. I have not heard that professional engineers are of the labouring class. I think there is a very vast difference between professional men and labouring men

Sir CHARLES H1BBERT TUPPER. One labours and the other does not.
That is the difference exactly.
I hope the Minister of Labour will not leave the chamber until he hears this argument.

The difference between the professional man and the labouring man is such as not to warrant the argument that the employment of foreign engineers is an interference with the rights of labour. Nobody more than the engineers themselves would resent being put in the same class as labourers. If we are talking of protecting the interests of labour let us do so, and if we are talking of protecting the professional men, let-us be honest about it and say so; but don't let us talk about protecting labour when we are protecting the professions.

1 notice that these same gentlemen who are so much excited about protecting the engineers who might get employment on the Grand Trunk Pacific, take no notice of the announcement made a few days ago that every foot of new railway to be constructed during the present year by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the Northwest is under contract to an American company. That meant that at least the men of responsible position with those contractors will be brought from the States. But the Canadian Pacific Railway is employing them and so it makes no difference. But in this case, if the Grand Trunk Pacific employs professional men from the United States, then the rights of labour are infringed upon, and the government must be denounced. I do not represent a labour constituency, but I am in favour of protection for labour such as it never received under the so-called national policy of the Conservative government. However, when it comes down to protecting professional men, we may afford to talk in a practical sense. Generally professional men are able to protect themselves. In this case we have a small class of professional men, engineers, in a large country. I want to see these professional men get a fair opportunity to join in this work, and in every other railway work in Canada, as we hope will be assured to them by the introduction of a general law, as has been suggested by the hon. gentleman from Vancouver Island (Mr. Ralph Smith). But I am not one of those who would maintain strongly that this country should not be allowed to go outside the very limited ranks of a particular profession fot the carrying on of a great public enterprise. If the contention is made that none but Canadian engineers shall be employed upon Canadian railroads, we are in the line of strengthening one of the closest corporations of professional men that ever cursed any country-and I am here to say that the corporations of professional men are a curse to this and all other countries where they exist. I make so bold as to say in this House, where there are so many professional men-and I do not think one of them will contradict me-that in both law and medicine the public are at the mercy of close corporations of professional men in every province of Canada. And if we are to be put under the same tyranny of professional engineers, when the country is face to face with a great enterprise, then it is something that I for one cannot join in endorsing. I am willing to give our engineers every kind of fair treatment; I am willing to support general legislation that will ensure fair play to them, but to consider them as a close corporation that we must deal with or not deal at all, I am not going to put myself in thafi position, let the cost be what it may. Let me say that this transcontinental railway enter-Mr. OLIVER.
prise means a great deal to the people of this country; it means a great deal to them whether it is well engineered or badly engineered. If we are supporting this arrangement under a proper impression, we believe the national treasury will not bear the burden. If we so believe, surely it is fair and right that those whose money will pay for this railroad shall have tihe opportunity to secure	the	best
talent to lay out the work.	Will that
not be more greatly in the general interest of the people of this country than any proposition to hand over the engineering of that great enterprise to a practically limited professional class organized into a close corporation, without any possible remedy ? We have all the close corporations of professional men we want ; and while we are prepared to give every reasonable advantage to our own Canadian engineers, I for one believe that they must stand on their merits and must expect that when an enterprise of such magnitude is being undertaken, the country wants the best, and that nothing but the best is good enough.
Does the hon. gentleman wish us to infer that the Canadian engineer is not equal to the American ?

I will not suggest that there are not Canadian engineers who are possibly superior to United States engineers ; but I will suggest that the United States, having 70,000,000 people and having thousands of miles of railroads to our hundreds, must necessarily have a great many more railroad engineers than we have, and that there is a fair possibility that out of the ten times greater number of engineers in the United States than there are in Canada, there may be a straggling few who may be better engineers than some of those in Canada; but that in any case if we want to get a large number of qualified, capable engineers to carry a great transcontinental enterprise through to completion in the shortest possible time, we may expect to go slightly beyond our own border, and there will be nothing very wonderful or deplorable about it.	.

The hon. member for Alberta knows that when they need a good engineer in the United States, for a coal mine, a gold mine or a railroad, they bring him from England or Germany. I know that from experience. Our engineers in Canada are just as good as those on the other side of the line. If we have not enough in Canada, we can go across the water and get more. There is no need of going to the States at an. We have just as good here as they have there, only we may not have so many ; but we do not need so many.

I might point out to the hon. member for Alberta that the Grand Trunk Pacific so far has only needed to hire surveyors and engineers ; and if this parliament and this government proves that it is

incapable of impressing the company with the necessity of making at least some pretense of employing Canadians in the first surreys, the prospects of Canadian labour getting anything like fair treatment when the actual employment of labour comes on will be very slim indeed. Of course, the hon. member sees that, otherwise I would imagine that he does not pay any particular attention to the gravity of the charges that have been made, to say nothing of their correctness. When this discussion started - this evening, the hon. Minister of Labour read a good deal of correspondence between himself and the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway Company; and one thing that occurred to me was that he was told practically that the Grand Trunk was too busy and could not be bothered. That is the usual kind of reply given to complaints of this kind. But the .point is this, that that kind of treatment is given to a minister of this country at the time this Bill of concessions is going through the House. That seems to me to be a very serious matter. It means at least that they are not afraid of us. It would seem to me that the only direction in which there is any celerity or willingness shown is in taking our money and our guarantees and asking for more. I am perfectly willing myself to aid in any general legislation covering this matter. I tried to do so at the time the Alien Labour Bill was before the House. But I think this matter should be settled with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company before we are asked to pass the third reading of the Bill. If it is done then, it will be done. It should be put in the contract as a matter of fact. I see by reference to last year's 'Hansard' that onSeptember 14 I proposed that it should be made a part of this contract that Canadian labour should be employed where it could be obtained and when it could be obtained. This matter of the employment of American surveyors and engineers was brought up at the same time, and if it had been taken up more seriously then, I believe a different state of affairs would exist to-day. However, the House is going to pass on this Bill next week, and it seems to me that it should be held up until the manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific gets time to communicate with the Minister of Labour.
